--- Getting TypeScript and Mongoose to Cooperate ---

At the end of last video, I mentioned that getting TypeScript and Mongoose to work together is sometimes
just a little bit awkward.
So in this video, I want to outline two big issues that we're going to run into.
Just so you are aware of why we were going to write out some slightly complicated code in just a moment.
So here's the big issue that we're going to start to run into.
First, I want to give you a quick review on some terminology around Mongoose and MongoDB inside of
MongoDB.
We organize information into different collections.
We might have a user collection that will store all the different users who have signed up for our application.
So in this case, users one through four.
Each of these can be thought of as little objects that stores some information about a very particular
user.
To access all this data, we're going to use Mongoose, and in particular, we are going to create two
different things inside of Mongoose.
We are first going to create something called a mongoose user model.
This is a class that is going to represent the entire collection of users.
So we will use this user model class to run queries, to create new users, or to do anything that modifies
or queries the overall collection.
We are also going to have something called a mongoose user document.
A user document is also a class.
It is meant to represent one singular user.
So we might create an instance of a user document to represent user number two or create a second instance
or another instance to represent just user number four.
So again, we've got a user model that represents all of our data and a user document that represents
just one little thing.
So at that quick refresher on terminology, here are the two issues that we're going to start to run
into when we are getting Mongoose and TypeScript to interact with each other.
So issue number one.
Is going to come up when we start to create a new user document.
So this is going to be how we eventually try to create a new user document or a new instance of a user.
We'll say new user and then pass in some different properties such as email and password.
Now whenever we try to pass in properties to anything, TypeScript wants to understand the properties
we are passing in and somehow make sure that you're passing in the correct type of data.
So TypeScript wants to understand the different arguments that calling new user is going to accept.
However, Mongoose does not make this easy behind the scenes, or more specifically with the Mongoose
type definition file that we just installed a little bit ago.
Whenever we try to create an instance of a user as you're doing right here, it is not going to kind
of tell TypeScript about the different properties that we are trying to pass in.
And so, for example, we could make a huge typo inside of here.
We could accidentally write in hard instead of password.
And TypeScript is not going to complain because TypeScript is not going to be given enough information
by Mongoose by default to understand the different types of arguments or the names of these properties
that we are supposed to pass in.
So this is issue number one that we are going to run into.
We have a workaround for this.
We're going to essentially somehow teach TypeScript about the different properties that this constructor
expects.
So we are going to solve this.
I just want you to be aware that this is something we need to be aware of.
Okay.
Issue number two.
So with issue number two, at some point in time, we are going to create a new user and we might assign
it some properties like, say, email and password.
That's then going to give us back a user document.
So that's, let's imagine right here, a user variable or something like that.
At some point in time later, we are going to want to access some of the data within this user.
Let's imagine for a second that we add in a console log of user.
If we did that, we might end up seeing that this user document has more properties than what we provided
to a constructor.
So for example, we might take that email and password and assign them as properties to user.
But behind the scenes, Mongoose might decide to add in a couple of additional properties as well.
Properties like let's say a created at timestamp or an updated at timestamp.
So the properties that we pass into the constructor don't necessarily match up with all the properties
that are created on the user document.
This is also an issue with TypeScript because TypeScript wants to know about all the properties that
exist on the user.
So we need to somehow tell TypeScript, Hey, look, we're going to pass some properties into the constructor.
TypeScript But don't worry, there are going to be some other properties that get created behind the
scenes and assigned to the user as well.
So we really need to teach TypeScript that there are kind of two different sets of properties.
There's one set of properties that will be passed to the constructor and there's going to be a second

That is issues number one.
And number two.
And again, this is some stuff that we're going to have to fight with around Mongoose and TypeScript.

--- Fundamental Authentication Strategies ---

We are finally to the last step of our sign up process.
So we are now considering a user to be signed in and that means we need to somehow generate a cookie
or a JSON web token, something like that, and send it back over to the user.
And the user should then use that token, that cookie, whatever it is to attempt to access other services
inside our application and prove that they are actually signed in.
Now, handling authentication, handling the process of making sure that someone is sending us a request
who is logged into our application is deceptively challenging in microservices.
So we're going to first start off with a little disclaimer here, handling it, user authentication.
So in other words, giving a user a cookie, a JSON web token or something similar and allowing them
to access other services inside of our app is a challenging problem that is not really solved.
In other words, there is not really a perfect solution to handling this stuff.
There is not some strategy where we just say, Oh yeah, use a cookie or use a JSON web token and try
everything works that doesn't exist.
So instead, with microservices and in the context of this course, I'm going to try to outline a couple
of different possible approaches in handling authentication approaches in how we can say, Hey, user,
here's a cookie, or here's a token of sorts.
Give this to us in the future and how we can decide whether or not a user truly is authenticated.
We're going to take a look at these different solutions, and I'm going to eventually show you one that
is going to work.
But it is definitely by no means perfect in nature.
Okay, so enough this disclaimer.
Let's get to it.
So.
I want you to imagine for a second that eventually inside of our application, which remember is all
about selling tickets and whatnot, that we will eventually have some kind of service called the Order
Service.
And inside this order service, the goal is to allow users to purchase a ticket.
So we can imagine that inside that service, we'll probably have something like ticket purchasing logic.
It'll probably be a request handler, something like that.
We could definitely imagine that at some point in time someone's going to send a request to the service
with the goal of purchasing a ticket.
Maybe in the body of the ticket, they'll have the ticket ID or the body the request or the ticket ID
or something like that.
And of course, along with this request, a user is going to have to prove that they are authenticated
with their application.
So along with the request, they're going to have to include some JSON Web token, some cookie or something
similar.
Something to say, I am signed in.
Then inside of our request handler, we are going to have to have some logic to say, is this person
actually signed in?
Did they give us a valid JSON web token?
Did they give us some cookie with some authentication information inside of it?
And we need to decide whether or not this person who's sending us this request is actually signed into
our app.
So this whole discussion we are about to have and this whole disclaimer right here about user authentication
really comes down to how we answer this question.
How do we decide whether or not someone is logged in in a microservices app?
This is way more challenging and deceptive than you would think.
So again, I'm going to show you two big approaches.
Here is approach number one.
Now on this first approach, I've labeled it fundamental option number one.
The reason I'm putting the word fundamental in here is that I'm going to show you two general approaches
to general strategies.
But there are very much variations of each of these.
At the end of the day, though, all the different strategies out there really come down to two very
fundamental principles.
That's why I'm calling this fundamental option number one.
Again, you're going to find variations of this, but it really comes down to this idea.
The idea is that we are going to allow individual services to rely on some centralized authentication
service to decide whether or not a user is logged in.
So let's again imagine that same scenario where someone's make your request to purchase a ticket.
It goes into our order service.
We then need to ask and decide whether or not this person is logged in.
So to answer that question with fundamental option number one, we might take that JSON web token or
that cookie or whatever else and send it in some synchronous request off to our authentication service.
And the authentication service might have some logic to take a look at that JSON web token, that cookie
or whatever else, and decide if this user is authenticated.
And so it would be up to the authentication service to send a response back over.
Now remember, I'm using the term here sync request not in the world of JavaScript, but in the world
of microservices.
In the world of microservices, sync request refers to a direct request from one service to another
one that does not make use of events or event buses or anything like that.
So the downside of fundamental option number one really shares all the same downsides as synchronous
communication in general.
If we put together this kind of solution right here, think about what would happen if the authentication
service just mysteriously went down one day.
If that thing crashed or just disappeared all of a sudden, no one, no service inside of our entire
application can decide if a person is logged in.
And that means that any request that requires us to decide if a person is authenticated is automatically
going to fail.
So by using this fundamental option, number one, well, we are going to be in a world of hurt if anything
goes wrong with our authentication service.
That's a very clear downside to fundamental option number one.
All right, let's move on.
I'm going to show you some other pros and cons as we go on.
But right now, let's just go on to the next option.
Now this is option 1.1.
So it's really the same as what we're just looking at, just about identical in nature, but we just
kind of move some stuff around.
At the end of the day, fundamental option number one is still very, very close to option number one
because we are still relying upon the service 100% of the time.
The only reason I'm showing you 1.1 right here is to help you understand that, yes, there are variations
in these strategies.
So with this strategy, we would say that any request coming into our application would need to go through
some central gateway of sorts that would authenticate the incoming request.
So whenever a user makes a request to purchase a ticket, rather than going directly to the order service,
we would instead have it flow into some authentication gateway or some authentication service of sorts
that would inspect that incoming request and decide if the user is authenticated.
If they are, we would then send the request along to the intended destination.
Otherwise we would just reject it right away.
This still shares a lot of the pros and cons of this option number one right here, because we still

Reliance on the authentication service.
In both cases, if this thing ever goes down or if this thing ever goes down, all of a sudden we cannot

Again, I'm only showing you this option 1.1 to say, yeah, there's variations on these things, but

With fundamental option.
Number two, we are going to teach each individual service how to decide whether or not a user is authenticated.

we are using and decide whether or not the user is authenticated.
So in this scenario, we have no dependency on outside services, no dependency on a gateway, some
other service or anything like that.
Everything is wrapped up inside of one single service, and if a user ever makes a request to this thing,
we will immediately and instantly know whether or not this user is logged in.
And so the upsides of this approach are very clear.
We do not have any outside dependency, as we did previously on this service.
If you give us a token and it's valid, hey, you must be logged in.
We're good to go and we will process your request.
So it immediately might seem like fundamental option number two is way better because we don't have
any outside dependency.
There is a very clear and immediate downside that you could probably imagine, and that is that we're
going to end up duplicating this authentication logic between all of our different services.
I want you to know right now that's not a big deal.
We could easily move this authentication logic into a shared library that's used among all of our services.
And so we can really just have very few implementations that get shared all over the place.
So I'm not really concerned about duplicating any of that logic, but there are some much more larger,
fundamental, very critical downsides of fundamental option number two.
And you really need to understand these because these the issues are and fundamental option number two
is where we are going to start to see that microservices communicating with each other is really, really
challenging.

Most importantly, biggest thing I want you to understand here and the biggest thing I want you to recall
is that JSON Web tokens and cookies are not the same thing.
They are not equivalent by any stretch of the imagination.
Let's take a look at a series of diagrams and just get a quick reminder on what a cookie is and what
a JSON web token is and how they are similar and how they are different.
Well, first begin with cookies.
So we're going to imagine that we've got some browser.
Making a request over to some server.
When the server sends a response back over to the browser, it can optionally include a header of set
cookie and then for that set cookie header, it can provide some kind of value.
This value right here can be a string that contains any information that we want.
That little piece of information is then going to be automatically stored inside of the browser.
Then whenever this browser makes a follow up request to the same domain with the same port, the browser
is going to make sure that it takes that little piece of information right there and appends it onto
the request as a cookie header.
So there's that little piece of information right there.
It will be automatically sent over to the server.
The key things to understand here around this cookie approach or this idea of saving some cookie is
that it's some arbitrary piece of information.
Doesn't really matter what this information is.
It can be anything we possibly can think of.
That piece of information will be automatically stored by the browser and automatically sent to the
server any time we make a follow up request.
Those are the key things to remember about cookies in general.
It's now off to JSON Web tokens.
So remember, with a JSON web token, we are going to take some arbitrary piece of information that
we refer to as the payload.
So this can be some kind of object that has maybe a user ID, a favorite color, just about any information
that we can possibly think of.
We're then going to take that payload and throw it into a JSON web token creation algorithm.
It's then going to spit out our JSON Web token that looks like an encoded string like this right here
or some kind of token.
Stored inside this thing is that original payload.
We can very easily take that string right there, throw it into some kind of decoding algorithm and
extract the original object.
So at any point in time, we can always access the information that is stored inside the token.
Once we have this token, we eventually do need to communicate it between the browser and the server.
There were a couple of different methods that we can do or use to actually do this communication.
So whenever the browser makes requests to the server, it's going to want to include that JSON web token
in one way or another so that the browser can prove that it is authenticated or it is logged in with
this particular server.
To communicate that token over some very common approaches are to include an authorization header that
has the JSON web token inside of it.
We can just throw the entire token inside the body of a request, assuming that it is a post request
or a put or a delete and so on.
Or alternatively, we can also kind of mix and match here and take that JSON web token and store it
inside of a cookie as well.
So the JSON web token will be managed automatically by the browser and included on all follow up requests.
All right.
So just to recap what we kind of recovered or recalled inside this video, differences between cookies
and JSON Web tokens.
Cookies are a transport mechanism.
They're a way of communicating information between the server and the browser, and they do not necessarily
do anything closely coupled to authorization.
We use them for authorization, but that's not necessarily the primary purpose of the primary goal of
them.
It's not the only thing they can do.
We can use cookies to move any kind of data between the browser and the server, so it doesn't have
to be authentication related stuff.
It can be tracking information.
It can be some kind of visit counter just about any kind of data we can easily store inside that cookie.
And then finally, cookies are automatically managed by the browser.
You and I, as developers specifically on the browser side of things, don't really have to worry about
managing managing them in any way, shape or form.
All you and I have to do on the server is set a cookie, and then we can be pretty much guaranteed that
we'll always come back in all follow up requests.
Jason Webb tokens, on the other hand, are all about authentication and authorization.
That is what they are intended to serve.
Inside of a JSON web token, we can store any form or structure of data that we want.
So it's traditionally going to be an object with some number of key value pairs.
And then Jason Webb tokens have to be managed manually by you and I as developers on the front end,
unless we are storing that JSON web token inside of a cookie.
All right.
So now that we've established the difference between these, again, I just want you to recall that
back inside this diagram where we said, oh, yeah, our authentication thing is a JSON web token or
a cookie.
It's kind of misleading to make these things sound equivalent because they are two very different things.
The cookie is just a transport mechanism.
It's something that's going to hold information.
It can be any kind of information.
It's not necessarily tied to authentication, JSON Web tokens.
On the other hand, traditionally all we use always used for authentication and authorization.

That would be probably not that great.
All right.
So let's summarize all this stuff up.
These are the requirements for our auth mechanism.
First off, we have to store information about a user, so maybe their user ID, their email or something
like that within the auth mechanism itself.
That is closely coupled with this last item down here.
So if we are storing information about that user, it has to be inside the auth mechanism and it must
not require us to have some kind of backing data store.
Next up, we have to be able to store some authorization info inside there as well.
So whether or not this person is an admin, a normal user or something else, we have to have a built
in and tamper resistant way.
So a user should not be able to mudie around with this or kind of fool us to expire or invalidate that
auth mechanism automatically without us having to reach out to a user's browser or something like that,
because we can't do that and try to invalidate their auth mechanism.
And then finally, whatever we choose has to be easily understood between these different languages.
So suffice it to say, all these requirements right here are very heavily steering us towards a JSON
web token approach.
The reason for this, it satisfies well, obviously, all these different issues right here, 100%,
Jason, Web tokens.
We can store any arbitrary information we want about a user.
There are even built in properties of JSON web tokens that lend to handling authorization very well.
Jason Webb tokens can encode expiration information.
They might be saying, Hey, Stephen, cookies can do that as well.
We can have cookies expire after a set period of time.
Well, not quite.
You see, we can set some expiration on a cookie, but that is us kind of politely asking a browser
to expire.
The cookie.
Cookie expiration is handled by the browser, so the browser is going to receive a cookie.
It's going to see that we ask the browser to expire that after, say, 20 days or something like that,
and after 20 days the browser will expire that cookie for us.
But a user could very easily copy that cookie information and just ignore the expiration date on there
and continue using that cookie in the auth mechanism or auth information side there at some point in
time in the future, even beyond that expiration date.
A JSON web token, however, is going to encode the expiration time in itself.
And as soon as the JSON web token expires, then that's it.
It will not be valid anymore.
Jason Webb tokens have fantastic support between different languages.
So every language out there, you're going to find an official implementation for handling JSON Web
tokens.
If we use solely cookie based authentication where we kind of create some kind of custom token and store
it inside of a cookie, it turns out that a lot of these different custom cookie implementations will
vary significantly between different languages.
And if you're super curious, I can even show you instances of that with some popular cookie libraries
used in the Node.js world.
It would be kind of hard to create a cookie that is signed securely, so it has some actual kind of
secure or encryption around it using Node.js or Express and then reuse that over in the Ruby on Rails
world.
That would be kind of challenging.
And then finally, Jason Webb tokens do not strictly require us to have some kind of backing data store
to identify this user.
Now as opposed to cookies.
You will see a lot of people who use cookies.
They're going to try to store, just say a session ID inside the cookie.
That refers to some session that is stored on a backend server that is not strictly required.
We can store again any arbitrary information we want inside of a cookie, but you're going to see that
a lot of people out there, a lot of methodology says that cookie based authentication, you're going
to store some kind of session ID.
And so of course, that does infer or imply that you will have a backing data store on the server,
which again, we probably do not want to do.
Okay.
So again, JSON, web token, that's what we're going to use now that makes it sound really easy.
And hey, these are great reasons for that, but we're still not quite done here.
Remember one thing we looked at earlier, when we decide to use a JSON web token, that's not the end
of the story.
Jason Web tokens are just an authentication mechanism.
They're a piece of data that proves that someone is logged in and stores some information about the
user.
We still have to somehow communicate this information between our browser and our server.
We can do it either manually to a degree using these headers or sticking it into the body of a request.
Or alternatively, we can have the browser handle it for us, using still this kind of cookie based
idea.
Now remember, this is where there really is a difference between cookies, cookie based authentication
and Jason Web tokens.
In this case, we're saying that we're going to use a JSON Web token to store our auth information,

That's how we actually shove or move the cookie around between the browser and the server.

Our React application is going to need to figure out whether or not the user is signed into our application.
The React application cannot directly look at the cookie and try to inspect and decide whether or not
there is a valid JSON web token inside there.
We have set up our cookies in such a way that they cannot be executed or accessed from JavaScript running
inside the browser.
So instead the React application needs to be able to make a request to something inside of our app to

user is or essentially whether or not the user is logged in.

Maybe if the user is not logged in, there will be no cookie, but if they are logged in, there will
be a cookie present.
So inside of our service or more specifically inside of this current user route handler, we're going
to take a look at that rec session, JWT property.
So remember, that is where we are going to see our JSON Web token show up.
So if the cookie is set, there will be a JSON web token there.
If the cookie is not set.
Chances are there will not be a JSON web token.
So we're going to then take a look at that property.
If it is not set or if for some reason the JSON web token is invalid.
Then we're going to return early and we're going to send back a response that looks like this.
Otherwise, if there is a JSON web token set on that session and the JSON Web token is valid, then
we're going to send back the payload that is stored inside the JSON web token.
So it's going to look something like this right here.
We're going to provide an object with a current user property.
And then for current user, we're going to put in the payload from the JSON web token.
So that's the general idea.
You'll notice I put in this diagram, I said if the JSON web token is invalid or valid.
So remember, at any given point in time, a user can technically try to mess around with their JSON
web token.
They can try to manipulate the information inside there and pretend that they are some other user or
change their email address or something like that.
But because we have set up this secure signature thing with JSON Web token, we're going to be able
to very easily detect if the JSON Web token has been manipulated in any way.

--- Scope of Testing ---

Our art service is now looking pretty good.
We've got all the custom air handling middleware routes.
It's all coming together.
But you might recall that when we first started this project, I had mentioned that we were going to
really put a good focus on testing.
And at this point, we have not done any automated testing.
We have done testing using Postman, but no automated tests.
So naturally we're going to start to fix that up inside the section.
We're going to first begin with a quick overview of how we handle testing in a microservices type environment.
The first big thing that we need to understand is that testing with microservices is really a big question
of what the scope of our tests are going to be.
So we're going to write out some code that is going to test our app in an automated fashion, and we
need to decide exactly what we are trying to test.
There's a wide variety or a wide spectrum of different things we can try to test inside of one single
test.
The list I have right here of four different things is by no means an exhaustive list.
I just want to point out that there are many different things we can try to test inside of a single
test go.
So we might first decide at the most basic level to test a single piece of code in isolation.
And so an example of that would be something like a middleware.
This would be a very traditional style of test, something you might refer to as a unit test.
The next level of complexity or the next kind of larger piece of scope would be to test how different
pieces of code work together.
An example of that would be maybe if we tried to simulate a request flowing through some different middleware
together and then eventually off to a route handler.
Now, as I go through these two notes right here, it might make a little bit more sense to kind of
visualize this.
So I put together a little diagram of more or less what our application looks like right now and some
parts to represent what it might look like in the future as well.
So we do not yet have an orders ticketing or payment service, but we will at some point.
So this first piece of scope right here would be if we were just trying to test one single piece of
code that might be like if we wrote out a test to just take a look at the required middleware and figure
out whether or not that thing is working correctly.
The next larger piece of scope would be to test multiple pieces of code working together.
And so that'd be kind of like if we had a request coming in and had it flow through the require auth
middleware and then up to some sign up root handler.
Now in this case, we're not going to ever wire up, require auth and sign up together.
I just mean to suggest that we could have a test that spans across different pieces of code.
The next larger piece of scope would be to test how multiple components work together.
Now I want to use the term component here.
I'm not referring to React.
I'm talking about different programs that we are running inside of our app.
So for example, that would be if we were trying to test how our service interacts with MongoDB or how
our service interacts with the event bus.
And then finally, the largest piece of scope, the largest thing we can really test in one go would
be to test how different services work together.
So, for example, we might try to launch our order service and the ticketing service at the exact same
time and then have one emit some kind of event and then expect it to be received by the other service
and for it to be processed in some very particular way.
So again, we really need to think about the scope of every test that we start to write out.
Now, of course, when we start to look at this list, you might say, or trend towards this item down
here at the bottom, you might say, Oh yeah, let's just test how all these different services work
together, because that kind of simulates reality.
Well, that might make a lot of sense when we say it.
We might want want to write tests like that.
But unfortunately, the reality is that writing tests like this is very, very complicated inside of
a microservices environment.
If we want to test how the order service and the ticketing service interact with each other, we need
to think about how to construct some kind of environment quickly and cost effectively to actually test
this stuff.
So, I mean, at a very practical level, how would we do that?
Would we launch some kind of test, Kubernetes cluster and then launch the order service and ticketing
service inside there?
How would we somehow issue requests to these things?
How would we somehow assert the result of any request we make?
It's just a very complicated thing that starts to get really challenging when we start to figure out
or try to figure out how multiple services work together.
So with that in mind, we are not going to focus too much on how we can test different services working
together.
Instead, we're going to try to test these different services, more or less in isolation.

--- Testing Goals ---

In this video, we're going to take a look at the different kinds of tests we're going to try to write
out for the different services inside of our ticketing project.

Instead, we're going to try to look at each service individually and test them one at a time.
So I want to show you the different kinds of tests that we're going to write as we are looking at,
say, just the OTT service by itself.
The first kind of test that we're going to write out is going to try to test basic request handling.
So, for example, we might want to try to make sure that if we make a request to our service to sign
up for something, then perhaps we should get back a response with a cookie that has the JSON web token
inside of it.
Or we might want to try to assert that we write some data into our MongoDB database.
So this is the first kind of test we're going to write.
We're going to make sure that we can issue a request to the service and then make sure that it gets
handled some in some very particular fashion.
The second test we're going to write is going to be more of a unit test style approach.
So the second test we're going to write might take a look at a very particular model inside of our app
and try to test some functionality around it.
This is not very relevant for the OTT service because our user model right now is very simple in nature.
But some of these services that we work on later will have models that are a little bit more complicated.
And so we are going to want to write some tests around them and make sure that they function in a very
particular way.
So again, the second kind of test we're going to write is going to take a look at individual models
and just try to make sure that they have some particular piece of functionality.
The final kind of test that we are going to write is going to handle the receiving and emitting of events
inside of our service.
At present, our service is not sending out or receiving any events, and we haven't even discussed
event handling inside this Kubernetes environment yet.
So we're not going to really worry about test goal number three either for the service, but for our
later services we put together, we will be writing out some code to make sure that we can receive incoming
events, to make sure that they get processed in some particular way, and to make sure that we can

--- Reminder on Server Side Rendering ---

We've now taken a look at the four different pages that we're going to create for this React application.
Remember, over time, we're going to add in a couple more pages to this thing for all the ticketing
features and aspects.
But right now our backend only supports authentication, so we're going to build out the React app to
support authentication.
All right.
So quick discussion on how we're going to actually build this thing.
Now on this diagram right here, this is a diagram we had seen previously.
This is how a normal traditional React application works in a development setting.
So in a development setting, we'll be running some kind of normal React app or really a React app development
server.
Any time a user types in a URL to their browser that's going to point them to a React application.
We're going to probably end up making at least two requests, but usually probably end up making three.
The very first request is going to fetch us an HTML file that is pretty much empty except for some very
basic script tags inside of it.
The browser will load up that HTML file.
It's going to see that some different script tags are listed inside there.
And so the browser will make a follow up request, possibly several requests to get some additional
JavaScript files that will be made to the Create React app development server that's going to respond
with the JavaScript files that the browser is asking for.
The browser will then execute all that JavaScript code or react application will start up and the React
app will possibly decide that it needs to make some follow up requests to fetch some data.
And so it might make a request to say the order service to get a list of orders.
The Order Service will then respond with that data and then the React app will take that data and render
some actual content on the screen.
So again, at least two, probably three or more requests just to show some content to a user.
So rather than taking this traditional approach, we're going to be using server side rendering instead
in a server side rendering approach.
The browser is going to make a request to our next JS development server.
Next JS is the framework we're going to use to implement the server side rendering stuff very easily.
The next JS development server is then going to internally make a couple of requests off to different
services to fetch some data.
So it might make a request over to the order service or the ticketing service to get a list of orders,
ticketing, whatever else.
The next jazz development server is then going to take that data.
It's going to build out a full HTML document, a document that has a ton of content rendered into it.
So perhaps some HTML to list out some orders or HTML to list out some tickets or whatever else.
It's then going to take that HTML and send it back to the user's browser all in one single request.
So there's several reasons we are making use of server side rendering here.
The first reason, and to be blunt, the most the most important reason for the context of this application
is I want to show you how to set up server side rendering in the context of microservices.
That's really why we are using next JS here, but there's several other reasons to do this.
First off, a user is going to see some content up here on the screen much more quickly.
Number two, a user is going to be able to see content more quickly, particularly if they're on a mobile
device.
So if a user is on a mobile device, they might not be able to load up all the JavaScript effectively
or in any timely fashion if we have a lot of complicated stuff going on in the screen.
And finally, server side rendered applications tend to fare a lot better with search engine optimization.
So these are all fantastic reasons to implement server side rendering inside of a kind of ticket purchasing
or e-commerce type application.
All right.
So now that we've got a quick reminder on how we're going to implement all this.

we are signed in in general.
So here's what we want to do.
We want to make sure that we make a request off to our service, specifically a request to the API users

of our application.

--- Options for Code Sharing ---

In this video, we're going to focus on how to build out this shared library.
We're going to first take a look at how we can somehow share code between multiple different services.
We're going to outline three different ways to share a code between the service and the ticket service.
Now, just be clear.
There are more than three ways to share code between projects, but we're going to be mostly focused
on these three different methods.
So method number one for sharing code between two projects is to just do a very direct copy paste.
So we could go into our service.
We could find all those middle where's all the custom air handling stuff and so on, and do a direct
copy paste of that code over to this new ticket service we're going to put together.
And there's definitely a very big downside to this approach.
If we start to copy paste stuff over, we might then go back over to our service and start to make changes
to this common code.
And so maybe we are now on version two over here.
How would we know what files changed?
How would we somehow get those files synced over to the ticket service?
We would have to do a direct copy paste again.
And when we did that direct copy paste, it might be really challenging for us to keep in mind exactly
what changed.
So it'd be kind of hard to document these changes over time.
I think you can probably we don't really need to spend a lot of time on this.
I think you can probably kind of instinctually sense that doing a direct copy paste this code between
projects is probably not the best way to do any kind of code sharing.
So I just want to mention it, but we're not really going to consider this as a serious option.
Met.
The number two is to use what is called a git sub module.
If you are familiar with git then you might have heard of sub modules.
A sub module is whenever we have one git repository and we want to somehow include another git repository
inside there.
So we might create a git repo for our service and our ticket service would then create a third repo
for all of our common code.
We would then add in this common repo into our off and tickets repos as a sub module.
And so you can imagine that we kind of take a copy of this thing.
And put it directly in right there and right there.
Now the upside to this approach is that we have all of these common code inside of version control.
And so we know at all times exactly what version of the common code we are running between these two
different projects.
We also have some really solid documentation on what gets changed between different versions.
The downside to this approach is that using get some modules in general is just a little bit challenging.
There's some different complicated commands whenever you create a new git repository.
Setting up some modules is always a little bit of a pain.
And so this definitely is a valid option, but there's just a little bit of pain associated with it.
So third option we're going to take a look at is publishing all this common code as an NPM package.
So this is what we are going to do.
We're going to take all this common code.
We're going to move it into a new project.
We're then going to publish this as a package to the NPM registry.
So we might give it a name of something like git ticks, dash common or something like that.
Then inside of each of our different services that need this common code, we will simply install it
as a NPM dependency using that same kind of NPM install command you are already familiar with.
The nice thing about this approach is that we can still version the code inside this common repository
or this common library.
So our service might use version 001 of this common library and a ticket service might use, say, version
002.
So if we ever start to make a change to this Git Ticks library, no problem.
We can still have all of our other services using the older version until we eventually get around to
making updates and adjusting them and saying, okay, let's now use version zero or two over inside
the service.
So we're going to use option number three right here.
Now, this definitely solves a lot of issues, but there are some really big downsides.
This means that any time that we want to change our common code, we're going to have to make our change,
push it up to the NPM registry, then go over to our different services and update our version to the
latest.
And that's just kind of a tedious process.
We are going to eventually write out a little script that's going to kind of automate some of the stuff
for us.
But I just want to point out that it is a little bit tedious and there will be times where we start
to write some code in an update to this common repository or this common library, and then we will
publish it.
We will update our ticket service with the newest version, and then we'll say, Oh my gosh, we just
made a little mistake.
So we'll have to go back over to the library, make the update, rebuild it, push it again, update
ticket service again.
In other words, there will be times where it's a little bit of a pain, but this kind of has the best
of all the different options.

--- NPM Organizations ---

In the last video, we established that we're going to share all of our code through an NPM package.

It might contain some very sensitive business logic or something similar.
And so before even creating this package, I just want to have a quick discussion on package security.
When we published a package with AMPM, there are really three different options or three very popular
options, I should say, available to us to make this package available to other people inside of our
company or other people who are working on our project.
We can publish this package to the NPM public registry.
We can publish it to the public registry inside of an organization, or we can publish it to a private
registry.
When we published a package directly to the public registry.
Anyone else can see this package by default, and so anyone else can take a look at your code and possibly
see your business logic inside their.
If you instead publish your package to a organization, we can mark the organization as public or assuming
it has private.
And then only people who are a member of this organization can see the packages inside.
If you want to use a private organization, you do have to pay extra money to NPM.
You can also create a private registry and access to this will be limited to whoever you give direct
access to.
If you try to create a private registry directly through NPM, you end up having to pay money.
Alternatively, you can also host your own open source version of a MPM registry which is free but requires
a bit of additional setup.
So in total, if we just publish this package directly to NPM, it will be public and visible to all.
If we publish it inside of a private organisation, it will be only accessible by people who are a member
of our organisation.
And if we publish it to a private registry, then only people who have access to our registry will be
able to see it.
We're going to end up going with the organization option.
So we're going to create a new organization and then publish our package inside there.
And just, you know, there are public and private organizations.
If you create a public organization, then everyone else is going to be able to see the package inside
of here.
It's only when we create a private one that the package will be hidden.

--- Big Notes on NATS Streaming ---

We've now gotten that streaming server up and running inside of our Kubernetes cluster.
In this video, I want to give you a quick overview on how Nat streaming server differs from that custom
event bus we had put together back in our first application, we're going to focus on some high level
items and then immediately after that, we're going to start to work on a very small, little stand
alone project to get a better idea of how we interact with that streaming server and some of its different
properties.
So let's get to it.
So we're going to take a look at a couple of different diagrams.
In every one of these diagrams, I'm going to show you something that our custom event bus so we had
previously built did and then we'll compare that to how that streaming server behaves.
The first thing I want to think about is how we communicated events between different things with that
custom event bus we had previously built.
So with the custom event bus, we might have had some service that would build up an event.
And then we use Axios to make a post request directly over to that custom event bus.
The Custom Event Bus was running a copy of Express, so it listened for incoming post requests.
It would receive that event and then internally take the event and make its own post request using Axios
out to some other service inside our application.
And those other services were running their own copies of Express that would listen for incoming events.
So this was a very simplistic approach where we basically relied upon the libraries of Axios and Express.
That was pretty much it.
Now that we're using that streaming server, however, we're not going to be using Express or Axios
to share events around our application.
Instead, we are going to use a client library that is specifically designed to work with Nat streaming
server.
The client library that we're going to use is called Node Nat's streaming.
Let's take a look at the documentation for it on NPM right now.
I'm going to open up a new browser tab and navigate to NPM chess.com.
Once here I will look up node nats streaming.
Here's the documentation for it.
Now, there's a lot of stuff in here that is just chock full of information.
There's a lot of stuff going on inside of here.
And unfortunately, whereas a lot of libraries out there, you can kind of just skim over it and say,
Oh, yeah, I know what's going on, and then reference it in the future any time some specific problem
comes up.
Unfortunately, with this library and that streaming server, it is kind of important to understand
the internals or how the stuff is really working from the get go.
So that's why we're going to do a little stand alone project to work just with that streaming server
by itself and not worry about any services or Kubernetes or anything like that.
We're going to have this little standalone project just we can understand these very important internal
mechanics.
They're going to be critical for us to use to properly communicate data throughout our application.
The one thing I do want to point out around this documentation right away, if you take a look at the
basic usage section, you'll notice that to work with this library, we've got a very event based kind
of architecture.
So in other words, if you're familiar with event emitter in Node.js or any other kind of eventing library
where we emit events and listen to them in plain JavaScript code, that is really how this library works.
So we're going to create some objects.
We're going to set up event listeners, and we're going to emit events as well.
It all works with a very heavily callback based kind of infrastructure.
So unfortunately we are going to be relying quite a bit on callbacks with this library as opposed to
using async await or anything like that.
All right, back over to our diagram.
So we're going to, like I said, be using no net streaming to create events, send them over to that
streaming server, and then that streaming server is going to send those out to our different services,
which will be listening for events, also using the node net streaming library.
So we're not going to have Axios or Express dedicated solely to handling events or anything like that.
We will of course still use Axios or Express for normal HTTP requests and so on.
I just mean to say that for all the event related stuff, we're going to be using node nets streaming.
Okay.
Second thing here.
So with our custom event bus.
Any time we emitted an event, that event was sent over to every single service.
So for example.
If we had our ticket service, emit an event of ticket update event.
We received it on our custom event plus and we send a copy of it off to our order service and whatever
other service.
Now of course we didn't actually have these services in our first application.
I just mean to say if we had to use this custom event plus in our current app, this is how it would
work.
So we would receive an event and throw it off to every different service.
Technically, even the service that had sent it to the event bus, the technically an event or the same
event went directly back to the ticket service, which was not super useful.
So as you guess, no doubt streaming is going to be very different in nature.
That streaming is going to require us to subscribe to specific channels.
So a channel, we're also going to use the term topic somewhat interchangeably.
These are essentially types of events or channels of events that we're going to be listening to specifically
inside of our different services.
So for example, on the NAT streaming server, we will create a collection of different topics or channels.
We're going to use that term pretty interchangeably.
Then whenever we want to emit some kind of event, we will create it inside of one service.
We will reach out to the node gnat streaming library and we will tell it.
Publish this event to the ticket colon updated channel so that event will be emitted out of our ticket
service.
It will go over to this channel on no net streaming and then the event will be sent along to only the
services that are listening on that very specific channel.
So for example, if our order service is listening for events on Ticket Colon updated, then it will
receive a copy of this event.
But if some other service, such as, say, payment service, was not listening to that channel, it
would not receive it.
So no longer does one event get sent everywhere.
Instead, we have to specifically say, here are the different topics or channels that we care about.
These are the different topics or channels that are going to exist, and then we have to specifically
subscribe to them inside of our different services to actually receive those events.
All right, onto the next diagram.
So next thing, back with our custom event bus.
We had put together a memory store of sorts to store all the different events that were ever emitted.
So, for example, if we had our ticket service, emit an event again of ticket updated, we would store
that inside of a in memory array.
It would of course also be emitted to all of our different services, but we held on to a copy of it
as well.
This feature right here was absolutely critical, so we could handle temporary downtime of any given
service if some service went offline for some very brief period of time.
It could then come back online and ask for a list of all the different events that had ever been emitted.
And so we could make sure that some service that was down for some period could come back online and
fetch or retrieve all the data or events it had missed during that period.
This is also fantastic.
For any time we needed to add in a new service.
So for example, if we decided to create a new service and add it into our application, maybe in this
case we called it payment service.
The payment service could then reach out to the event boss and say, Hey, give me a listing of all
the different events that have ever been emitted.
So we could then take our big list of events, send them all down, and then the payment service or
whatever news service this is, would then be magically and suddenly up to date with all the relevant
data inside of our app.
So this idea of storing memory or storing events somehow was really critical for handling outages or
handling any new service we pulled up as well.
Now streaming server has a very similar idea, but it's way more complex and robust.
So the net streaming server, it's going to store all the different events that get emitted in memory
by default.
However, we can also customize it to store these events inside of flat files stored on a hard drive
or even inside of a database like MySQL or post grass.
So again, for example, ticket service could emit an event over to that streaming server.
It will be stored inside of memory.
And simultaneously a copy of that event will be sent out to all the relevant services.
If we then at some point in time bring a payment service or some new service online, it can reach out
to that streaming server, ask for a copy of all the different events, and that streaming server will
respond with all the relevant events that it has missed out on.
So the same thing is true if we decide to store all these events on a flat file, MySQL database or
post grass as well.
So I'm not going to go through drawing out the entire diagram.
I think you get the idea here.
If we might emit an event over to that streaming server, we can configure it so these these events
get stored inside of some file or database.
So now if our NAT streaming server server ever goes offline or has to be restarted, of course it loses
everything stored in memory.
But if we stored those events inside of a file or database, then after the Nat streaming server comes
back online, it could connect to that database or that file.
Take a look at it and say, Oh, okay, here's all the different events that have ever been emitted.
Okay.
So that is it.
Those are some very high level notes on some critical differences between our event bus and Nats streaming
server.
So the big ticket items here are that we're going to use this custom little client library called no
net streaming to communicate.
Next up with not streaming, we have to create these things that are called topics or we're also going
to use the term channels for them and then our services have to specifically subscribe to events from
these specific channels.
And then finally, very similar to our custom event, plus we can have Nat streaming server store all
these events in memory or alternatively store them inside of a file or database as well.
So now that we understand some of these very core differences, we're going to take a pause right here
and start writing some code in the next video.

--- Queue Groups ---

Well, maybe.
Let's think back to the earlier project we worked on inside this course.
I'm going to open up my code editor very quickly.
Back on that blog project directory.
Okay.
So you might remember working on the blog project inside of here, we allowed users to create posts
and comments.
One big problem we ran into was making sure that we could make one single request and get all of our
posts and all of our comments all inside of one request.
To allow for that, we created something called the query service.
And inside the query service we had some code that would receive events.
We then processed all those events inside of this handle event function.
We had some code inside there to handle post created, comment created and comment updated.
But there's one event type that I want to focus on in great detail.
The comment created event.
So whenever we got an event of type comment created, we took a look at the ID of that incoming event
or the post ID in this case.
We found the post that we had previously saved.
We then took a look at all the comments that we had associated with it, and then we pushed in a brand
new object representing that comment.
Now for a second, let's just imagine that we were not storing these posts in memory.
Let's imagine instead that we are storing these posts inside of some kind of MongoDB database or some
other similar kind of database.
So let's imagine what would happen if we ran this code right here.
Or something like that.
On two separate instances of this query service.
Well, we would take the incoming event.
We would pull off the ID content and status, and then we would add that in as a brand new comment inside
of our list of comments.
So what would happen if we essentially ran that line of code twice?
Well, very simple.
We would end up with the same exact comment twice inside this comments array.
So very frequently.
We do not want to allow an incoming event to go off to every copy of every service that we have.

--- Common Event Definitions Summary ---

I think this little test with Nats streaming server and putting together this little test project has
had some pretty good results.
So we've now got this space listener, base publisher.
We got the listing of all of our different subjects.
We've seen how to create a event that describes some message we're going to send out and how to create
the custom publisher and listener as well.
So at this point, we're going to start to wrap things up and move forward.
But I do want to do a very quick summary and really touch on two items really quick.
So first off, thinking about how to test these things.
When we think about testing the publishers, the publishers themselves are actually rather similar to
making a plain network request.
In other words, it's rather similar to using something like Axios.
We're essentially using this class to make a request or publish some information.
There's not really going to be a lot of business logic inside these, and so we're not really going
to focus a whole bunch on how to test them.
Listeners, on the other hand, are a totally different story.
The listeners we put together are going to receive events, and the assumption here is that we're going
to do a lot of business logic or processing on these incoming events.
In that regard, these listeners are actually similar in nature to request handlers, and we're definitely
going to want to do a lot of testing around the listeners we put together and make sure that we handle
everything inside them correctly.
So we will be spending a lot of time to figure out how to write some tests effectively for a listener.
Okay.
One other quick item.
So at this point, I just want to highlight that we have centralized a ton of information into our common
module.
The common module is now going to be the primary source for where we define all of our different event
names or remember what they are called in the world of networks.
They are subjects.
Inside of here.
We also had the exact definition of what all of our different events are going to consist of.
So the subject for each of them and the data that these events are going to contain.
We are not going to define any events whatsoever inside of our different services.
Instead, we are going to import them from this common module.
And this is going to absolutely, positively ensure that all of our services are using the same event
names, and the data inside of them will always be consistent.
Now a quick side note, kind of like a higher level note here.
When I was first putting this course together, I've worked on this course for a extremely long time
at this point.
A very long time.
And the vast majority of that time was actually evaluating different options on how to put this common
module together.
And when I was really thinking about building this course and going through all that work, I thought
this section where we were talking about building out this custom event, handling stuff in the common
module, was going to be like a huge deal and it ended up being just about 14 videos or so.
I'm kind of shocked at how things actually turned out.
Anyways, back on topic here.
The reason that's really relevant is that I really cannot understate how important it is to put the
definition of all these events and these event names into some common location.
It is simply not feasible to only define these events inside of your services because as I've said several
times, you are going to make typos on event names and you are going to make typos on property names
as well.
It is guaranteed I 100% guarantee it if you try to define these things directly inside of your services.
And that's why putting it all inside of some common module is so, so helpful.
I almost wish that we hadn't put the common module together from the get go so that we could have experienced
the pain of having to guess these property names and have to go look them up back and forth.
And all that pain, I think, would have given us a lot more appreciation for defining the events inside
of here.
Now, I do want to say there is a downside to this approach.
We are writing TypeScript code, putting these event definitions inside of a TypeScript module.
So naturally, this whole approach right now is only going to work if all of our different services
are written with TypeScript.
If we have some other service using Java or something like that, well, this shared definition of what
an event is is not going to be quite so useful if you do expect to have services with other languages
being used inside them and you don't expect to be able to use some kind of common module.
All written TypeScript.
There are a couple of options.
So if you want to have a common definition of all the events, the information inside them, and share
it inside of some kind of polyglot architecture, you can take a look at some other alternatives, such
as JSON schema.
JSON schema allows you to define JSON structures, the different properties they'll have, the different
values they'll have, and some validation around those properties.
And this can be done in a cross language way.
In other words, a lot of languages have support for JSON schema.
So you can write your JSON schema inside of some kind of common repository.
So maybe a GitHub repo or something like that.
So you can easily work with it between different languages.
And then each year different services can pull in those JSON schema files and use them to validate events
that they're trying to publish.
Another alternative is proto buff.
Proto buff is a way of serializing information, not unlike JSON, but it compacts information into
a much more compact format.
Heard above can be used to define the structures.
It also has cross language support.
Finally, there's also something else called Apache Avro.
This is really themed around Java in particular, but there is support for a variety of different languages
as well.
It's just not as strong as the Java focused side.
So again, if you do expect to have some multi language services inside of your application rather than
doing a common module with TypeScript and putting the event definitions in there, you might take a
look at these approaches.
Just so you know, I did originally kind of tried to design this application using JSON schema.
I also did a version of it with Proto Buff as well.
Neither of them were anywhere near as usable as the TypeScript implementation we ended up with.
So I showed you the TypeScript solution because I really did believe it was a very good way of handling
this and avoided a lot of headaches that we would have ran into if we tried to make use of JSON schema
or proto buff.
So just throwing that out there.

--- Failed Event Publishing ---

I'm taking a look at our new ticket route handler and the update route handler.
And between the two of these, they have pretty similar logic.
A request comes in, we do some validation, we make some changes to a ticket document, save it, and
then publish an event that's inside of update, very similar inside of New.
We do some validation.
We create a ticket document, save it, publish the event.
But you might notice a very small difference between these two route handlers, and that is the presence
of the await keyword on the publisher in each of them.
So inside of my new route handler, I have the await keyword on ticket created publisher.
But inside of update I did not place that await keyword.
This is to highlight a very interesting little issue that we might run into once our application starts
to scale up.
So let's take a look at a couple of diagrams and really understand what the presence of that awake keyword
does for us.
So here's what goes on behind the scenes inside of our ticket.
Created Handler.
So inside there, we're going to create a ticket document.
We're then going to await that ticket being saved to the database.
And because we've got that awake keyword on the ticket, save call right here, that means we're going
to essentially sit around and wait for that record to be saved to the database before we continue execution
of this function.
So after everything gets saved, then we move on to the publisher.
And because we've got the awake keyword on that publisher, we're going to wait for the event to be
published.
And that's and then eventually we're going to send a response off to the user.
Now let's start to think about what would happen if something went wrong with this event publishing
process, or for that matter, if something went wrong with saving the record to the database as well.
So because we've got the awake keyword on there, if anything goes wrong with either saving the record
to the database or publishing the event.
If we ever throw an error of any sorts from either of those lines of code, that air is going to be
caught and handled by our air handling middleware.
So the air handling middleware is going to inspect that air, come up with some likely response or good
response and send it back to the user.
The point is, if anything goes wrong, the user is going to know about it.
Let's think about what would happen inside of our update handler, which does not have the a keyword
on the publisher.
In that scenario.
Here's what would go on.
So here's the update handler.
We have some logic inside there to make an update to the ticket document.
We then await saving the ticket to the document database.
So in that scenario, once again, if anything goes wrong with saving the ticket, well, air is going
to be thrown and it will be caught by our error handling middleware.
But then right after that, we try to publish an event to Nats.
And then immediately after that, because we do not await that publish.
So immediately after we attempt to publish that event, we then send a response directly to the user.
So we can really imagine inside this update handler, this line of code runs and then essentially in
the next microsecond, we then immediately send a response back to the user.
That means that if anything goes wrong with publishing this event to Nets, we don't get any opportunity
to tell the user that some error occurred with the request.
So what starts to get really interesting, however, is whether we actually need to tell the user that
something went wrong with a published event.
If we think about this really back inside the new request handler, it might sound like a pretty obvious
thing.
Hey, let's await the event to be published so that the user knows, hey, everything went as expected.
But does a user really care about this event being published?
All we're really doing here is adding in some arbitrary latency latency to our request, as we have
to await our net's client to reach out to the that server, publish the event and get some response
that says, Hey, event published successfully.
So this really does add in some tiny bit of latency to the request.
Now, what's way more relevant than all this stuff, though?
Whether or not we await for the request or not is, well, what really happens behind the scenes if
publishing an event fails?
Let's expand on that a little bit more.
I want to show you another diagram that's going to kind of show you that this entire idea of whether
or not we await publishing the event is not super relevant because there's actually a way bigger issue
for us to start to think about.

So here's the diagram right here.
A little bit crazy.
It is similar in nature to several we've already looked at.

We successfully saved the transaction to the database.

Well, if we can really think about it in terms of some banking application, we would have a very critical

--- Handling Publish Failures ---

In the last video we saw that we can get into some really big trouble if we ever successfully save a
record to the database and then fail to emit an event describing that record we just saved.
So we would not update this other database or this other service over here, and a user would see some
really strange data inside of our app.
So how can we solve this?
Well, luckily, there's a somewhat straightforward approach to this, pretty straightforward.
And it's going to work vast majority of the time to make sure that we don't run into any really big
issues.
So here's the idea.
So as in the diagram we were just looking at in the code that we currently have, we have seen that
whenever we save record to the database, we're then going to immediately emit an event or publish it
over to our event bus to solve this whole issue.
Rather than emitting an event over to the event bus, we're going to instead save that event into our
database.
So we're going to still take some record in this case, a transaction or whatever, a ticket, whatever
it is, save it into our database and we're going to simultaneously take the event that we want to emit.
And rather than emitting it, we're going to save it into some kind of events collection inside of our
database as well.
Then along with that event, we're going to record some kind of flag on whether the event has actually
been published.
When we first saved this thing into the database, no, the event has not yet been published.
So we would say no, it has not been sent.
Then inside of some separate process or some separate piece of code, something outside of our root
handler, we can then have some code that is watching this events collection and it can take note of
any time we save a new event into it.
Any time we save a new event into this events collection, this separate piece of code can then extract
that event, essentially pull it out of that collection and publish it off to nets.
Once it successfully gets published, we can then update this sent flag over to.
Yes, this event has been published.
So this kind of two stage approach is going to go a long way to solving this entire issue.
If there's ever some issue connecting to our database, well then we will fail to save this transaction
and the event.
And so we will not have any data integrity issues.
If Nats is down or if our connection to Nats is down for some crazy reason, we can still save the ticket
to the database or save the transaction to the database, save the event, and then hopefully at some
future point in time when our Nats connection comes back up, this separate piece of code or process
or whatever else can still pull this event out and publish it off to Nats.
This approach really makes sure that we're not going to run into this issue where we save a record and
fail to publish some data around it.
There is one other thing to imagine.
However, there might be some kind of crazy possibility where we successfully save this transaction
in and then maybe fail to save the event.
Maybe we fail to save the event because there is some kind of database constraint or something like
that.
So we really need to make sure that whenever we save a transaction, if that gets saved, we have to
make sure that the event gets successfully saved as well.
And of saving either things, things fail, then we need to make sure that we undo all the changes that
we have made to the database.
So in other words, if we successfully save the transaction but not the event, we need to make sure,
sure we roll back saving the transaction.
And if we save the transaction or save the event but not the transaction, we need to make sure we roll
back saving the event as well.
So to do something like this, a lot of databases have something like this already built in.
Even MongoDB does.
This is the idea of something called a database transaction.
Now, let me pause right here and say that we have the word transaction on this diagram twice.
And these are two very different transactions.
So inside of this database, this transactions collection, is talking about a user depositing some
money or something like that.
That is some very application specific behavior.
A lot of databases, on the other hand.
So this is the other use of the word transaction.
A lot of databases implement a feature called a transaction, and a database transaction is something
that allows us to say there is a set of changes that we want to make to our database and if any of these
changes fail, do not make any of the changes.
So we can wrap up saving this record and saving the event inside of a database transaction and of saving
either of these things fails.
The database will automatically roll back all these changes.
So a database transaction will ensure that we always save the record and the event along with it successfully
or both them will fail.
So again, that's how we're going to solve this issue.
Now, you might recall earlier on inside this course, I said that I wanted to build this application
as realistically and production grade as possible, but that we were going to cut one or two corners.
So this entire system right here of saving an event into the database and publishing it later on and
this entire idea of a database transaction, this is where I'm kind of drawing the line for the course.
We are not going to implement this inside of our application just because it adds in a pretty good amount
of complexity.
And to be honest with you, I don't really anticipate us to ever really have to deal with an issue around
saving a record to the database and then possibly not successfully saving some or publishing some information
over to nets.
So I just don't really think we are going to experience this issue inside of our application.
And I don't really expect that we will ever even be able to effectively test that or test this realistically
as well.
We could definitely write some kind of automated test to make sure that this thing works as expected,
but I just don't really expect us to be able to test it in any realistic scenario.
So we are not going to implement this inside this application.
But I just wanted you to know that this is a concern and it's something that you might want to write
some code to handle.
Again, we could save it or deal with this issue by saving the record and the event at the same time
have the separate process to pull events out of that events collection, publish them off to nets.
And we would probably want to also make sure that we wrap up saving the record and the event inside
of some transaction as well.
Ooh.
Okay.
So that's that, as usual.
Quick pause right here.
