--- Orders Service Events ---

We've got our full list of handlers put together inside of our order service.
So we're now going to start to think about adding in support for events to this thing as well.
In total, our order service is going to emit two kinds of events.
You might remember that we still have that PDF from a couple of videos ago when we were originally talking
about Nats.
This PDF listed out all the different events we are going to eventually publish and we had said that
the Order Service was going to publish events of order created and order cancelled.
So let's take a look at the reason that we are implementing both those events.
First off is order created.
The goal of order created is to tell every other service that, well, an order has just been created.
Let's take a look at why each of these different services needs to know about this order being created,
because it turns out that on this event, we're going to have to emit a very particular piece of data.
We'll start off first at the payment service.
The payment service needs to know that there's going to be some kind of new order and that some user
might attempt to submit some payment in the form of a credit card or something like that.
So the payment service needs to know about order created for two very important reasons.
First, it needs to know just that there is an order that needs to be paid because eventually when the
user tries to submit that credit card, they're going to also include the ID of the order that they
are trying to pay for.
The payments service just needs to know, Hey, here's some ID of an order and I should receive payment
for this.
But the payment service also needs to know very critically how much that order costs.
So it needs to know that it's going to receive a payment for some amount of money.
The order service or the order itself doesn't actually know about how much the order costs.
Instead, it is the embedded ticket that is inside the order that is going to tell us how much the order
needs to be paid for.
So that's why we are communicating this information over the payment service order created is also going
to go over to the expiration service so we can start up that 15 minute timer.
Now, remember, it's not necessarily 15 minutes per say.
Instead, the order itself has an expiration time already marked on it.
It's got that expires at flag.
So we just need to make sure that order created communicates that expiration time over to the expiration
service so that the expiration service can eventually say after 15 minutes or however long it is, hey,
this order should now be expired.
And then finally and this one's a little bit confusing.
The ticket service also needs to know when an order has been created.
And the reason for that is that the ticket service needs to somehow lock down a ticket and prevent editing.
So imagine the case in which an order or a user goes to purchase a ticket when the ticket costs $20,
and then maybe right after the user creates the order, maybe say 2 minutes after the person who is
selling the ticket goes to the ticket service and adjust the price of that ticket to $2,000.
We definitely want to prevent that from happening.
So once an order has been created and a ticket has been reserved, we need to somehow make sure that
a ticket cannot be edited.
So we're going to do so by making sure that this order created event goes over to the ticket service.
The ticket service is going to accept that event.
It's going to somehow lock down a ticket from further editing until eventually the order is either paid
for or canceled.
That's it for order created.
The other event that this thing is going to emit is order canceled.
And this one's a little bit more predictable.
So order canceled.
That's pretty much going to reserve a ticket from the ticket service, which means that the ticket can
be edited again and the person who owns the ticket can change the price or the title or whatever else.
Order canceled is also going to go over to the payment service.
This is just to tell the payment service that it should reject any further payments that are made for
this order.
And technically, this is also going to handle refunds as well.
You'll see example of that later on.

So for me, I'm currently in Mountain Standard Time, so it would be some date time right here, Mountain
Standard Time, and that's not what we want.
Whenever we share time stamps across different services, we want to communicate them in some kind of
timezone, agnostic sort of way.
So ideally we would be providing a UTC timestamp which is going to work regardless of what the time
zone of the service that is receiving this event is in.
So rather than relying upon this default to string behavior of the date object, which would end up
with some not time zone that we want, we are going to instead control how this thing gets turned into
a string.

And that's how we do it.
That's how we get a UTC timestamp.
Notice how it's capital ISO and A capital S.

--- Optimistic Concurrency Control ---

In this video, we're going to get a better idea of how Mongoose and MongoDB collaborate to set up and
use this version field stuff.
All right.
First thing I'm going to do is take a look at how Mongoose and MongoDB normally collaborate to handle
record updates.
So this is without this version flag or anything like that.
So inside of our ticket service, we might have some code that's going to fetch record CC.
Q We might then run some update on the document.
So, for example, set its price to ten or 15 or whatever else.
Well, then tell Mongoose to save the document.
And very critically, when that occurs, Mongoose is going to reach out to MongoDB and it's going to
tell MongoDB, Hey, I want you to do an update on record CPQ.
So it's going to send off some kind of request to MongoDB.
And the very critical part here is that inside this request there's something that says find the record
with ID queue and set its price to ten.
So MongoDB internally is going to look at its collection of tickets.
It's going to find a record with IDC's queue and then update its price to ten.
And that's it.
That's the entire process.
Another thing I really want to emphasize here is that in the request to update this record, there's
something that says Find specifically the record with ID.
Q So with all that in mind, let's now take a look at the same flow.
But with all this version tracking stuff enabled, we're going to see how Mongoose and MongoDB collaborate
to make sure that we only update records with the appropriate version number.
Okay.
So same kind of flow here.
But now we're imagining that this version of field thing is being incorporated or included.
Now, just, you know, this entire process that we're going through is referred to as optimistic concurrency
control.
And if you want to, you could do a quick Google search, take a look at a blog post or two and read
a little bit more about it.
The entire strategy that we're talking about here for optimistic concurrency control at MongoDB is 100%
applicable to other types of databases as well.
So what we're discussing here is not isolated to MongoDB.
This is not a MongoDB specific strategy.
You can use the strategy with many other types of databases very easily.
Okay.
So in this flow, we're going to once again fetch a record from Q, run a update on the document, save
the document, and then internally we're going to turn a setting on inside a mongoose that's going to
cause mongoose to automatically update the version field of the document automatically.
So that would be where we increment the version field from, say, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4 or whatever
else Mongoose is.
Then once again going to send an update request off to MongoDB.
And now, now that we are implementing this versioning stuff, here is the critical, critical difference
inside this request.
Mongoose is going to tell MongoDB to find the record with IDC's Q and a version of one and set its price
to ten.
That is the critical little step.
So whenever MongoDB tries to update a record, it's not actually going to try to compare these version
numbers and say, Hey, is this less than one or is this less than the current version number or whatever
else that doesn't actually occur?
What really happens is Mongoose is going to say, find the record with this particular ID and this particular
version.
So it's in how we find this record that's going to make sure that we select some record with the correct
version.
Now let's imagine the scenario in which we do have a record inside of our database with an idea and
a version of one.
We would find this record right here.
It has the correct ID and the correct version, and we would set its price to ten and that's it.
Everyone is happy now.
What would happen if something goes not quite right?
Well, I'm going to roll this back and let's imagine that we accidentally process the $15 price update
first.
So that would have been the event that we discussed just a moment ago.
This one right here where we're trying to set the price to 15 and we would be looking for a record inside
of our database with a version of two because this thing has a version of three.
So in that scenario, this query right here would instead say, find the record with IDC's Q and A version
of two and set its price to 15.
Now, as you can guess, MongoDB is going to run a query over the tickets collection.
It's going to look for a record with a ID of Q and a version of two so we can look through all these
records.
And there's no record that matches that query.
There's no record with an idea.
CC Q And a version of two.
There is one with an ID Q and a version of one, but that's not what we're asking for.
We're asking for one with a version specifically of two.
And so this request right here, this update would fail and this error would be returned to our application
where we would be forced to deal with it in some fashion.
But that's it.
That is what is going on behind the scenes.
It's really all hinging upon the fact that when we send over these requests to update a record, we're
including not only the idea of the record we're trying to update, but also the version of the record
we're trying to update as well.
And that is what is used for the criteria to find the record that we're trying to make a change to.
Now, one thing you'll notice here is that this is all about updating records.
It's not about inserting records.
So the assumption is that when we first insert a record, it's always going to default to a version
of zero or one.
So we don't really run into big issues with inserting records.
Not really a big concurrency issue there.
It's a bigger issue when we're trying to update existing records.
That's when we start to get into big trouble, and that's where this version flag is going to start
to become really, really handy.
Okay.
So that's it.
That's the idea.
So as you guess, well, we have to make a little change or two to Mongoose.

--- Who Updates Versions? ---

We're now going to go back over to our common module and inside of all the different events we have
created inside of here.
We're going to make sure that we communicate the version number inside of these things.
So, for example, in the case of ticket updated, along with some information about the ticket that

to eventually help us make sure that we process these events in the correct order.
Before we add in this version number, however, I want to try to answer a question that you might be
asking yourself right now, and that question might be something like this When should we increment
or include the version number of a record with an event?
Should it be all the time?
Should every single event that ever talks about some record always increment a version number or always
include it?
The answer is no.
We are only going to worry about incrementing or including the version number of a record whenever it
is the primary service responsible for a record that is emitting an event to describe that record either
being created, updated or destroyed.
Now, this rule alone by itself doesn't really make a lot of sense and I don't think really answers
this question.

--- [Optional] Versioning Without Update-If-Current ---

This is going to be a optional video, 100% optional.
So if you just want to stay focused on the topic at hand, pause the video right now and continue on.
Otherwise, stick around and I'll tell you what we're going to discuss in this video.
So I want you to notice how between our ticket service and the order service, we use that exact same
module to manage all that versioning stuff.
So we made use in both services.
Of that module called Mongoose Update if current.
Now, to be honest with you, that was kind of cheating.
We are kind of cheating by using this module inside of both these different services.
Let me tell you why.
By using this service or that module, we are able to assume that this orders database right here in
all the tickets inside of it are essentially going to manage themselves.
So in other words, whenever we have some incoming event, come in.
We're going to go through that process of subtracting the version number to find the appropriate record.
We then apply some updates to that record.
And then specifically, the real gotcha here is that this module, when we save the updated ticket,
it is going to take the version number right here already inside of our database and increment it by
one.
So that module alone is responsible for updating the version number inside of our orders database right
now.
Is that a bad thing?
Well, I would argue, yes, it is.
And here's why.
Right now, we are 100% aware of where these events are coming from.
We know they are coming from the ticket service and we know exactly how the version numbers work inside
that ticket service.
We know that they start off at zero and they are incremented by one every single time.
So we are able to make use of the mongoose update if current module inside the order service just because
it matches the exact same versioning semantics as the ticket service.
But there might be some kind of scenario out there at some future point in time where these ticket updated
events are coming from a totally different kind of database.
Maybe it's not a mongo database.
Maybe it's something that doesn't use Mongoose.
It might be a totally different kind of information store.
And with these other kinds of information stores, we cannot necessarily always rely on them using the
exact same versioning semantics as this mongoose mongoose update if current module.
So inside of some alternate universe, we might have these events coming in from some other part of
our application we don't really know, and they still might look identical.
So they're still ticket created, ticket updated, tick up, ticket updated.
But they might have an entirely different schema for applying versioning numbers.
So they might start off with a version number of 100 and then increment by 100 for every successive
version.
And if that was the case, we could definitely not make use of this very easy to use module inside of
our order service because it is always assuming that our versioning starts off at zero and increments
by one every single time an update is issued.
Besides having this very different kind of versioning, where we start off at 100 increment by 100 every
single time, there might be some other database that's emitting these events or some other service
that's emitting these events.
And they might use a version that is a timestamp to indicate when this record was saved.
And so once again, maybe that time stamp doesn't work too well with the Mongoose plugin we are using
the mongoose plug in we are using does technically support time stamps, but let's imagine for whatever
reason, these time stamps are not interoperable.
For some reason.

--- Listeners in the Tickets Service ---

So what are we going to work on next?
Well, at this point in time, we have wired up our order service that is listening to the ticket created
event and the ticket updated events.
So Order Service is processing those events pretty darn well.
The order service in turn is also emitting a couple events.
So for example, the order service is publishing order created and order canceled.
We need to now make sure that the ticket service is going to have a listener that's going to watch for
the order created event and the order canceled event.
The reason for this, remember, is we need to make sure that we lock down a ticket after an order has
been created for it.
So once a ticket has been reserved, the ticket service needs to make sure that the person who owns
this ticket, the person who created the ticket, cannot come back and start to edit it because we don't
want a user to start to go through the process of purchasing a ticket and then see the price just mysteriously
change or the description change or anything like that.
So to implement that, we're going to go back over to our ticket service.
We're going to implement two different listeners.
Whenever the ticket service sees a list or an event of order created, we're going to find the appropriate
ticket inside the ticket service and set something on there that's going to lock down that ticket and
prevent us from making any further changes to it.
Then whenever we see an order canceled event which indicates that the person who's trying to buy the
ticket says, forget this, I don't want the ticket, or maybe the order times out or whatever else.
We're then going to make sure that we unreserved the ticket or essentially unlock it down and allow
editing of the ticket once again.
So that's pretty much it.
It's pretty much an on off lag.
Whenever we see what are created, lock the ticket.
Whenever we see cancelled, unlock the ticket, that's all it is.
So not the worst thing in the world.
Now that we've got an idea of what we're doing, pause right here, start to implement this in the next
video.

--- Strategies for Locking a Ticket ---

We're inside of our order created listener.

But I'm going to suggest maybe if we start to think forward a little bit about some other capabilities
that we're going to maybe eventually want to have inside of our application, we will realize that just
having a simple Boolean, maybe not the best thing in the world.
So I want you to imagine the following scenario.
If we made use of some simple boolean to track whether or not a ticket is locked.

No clue what so whatsoever.

the class, even in a child class.

We could instead mark as protected.
If we mark it as protected, that means that the child class of order created listener can access that
property.
It can access the client, take the client and pass it off to the ticket.
Updated Publisher.
And so this would be a way preferable solution because it's going to make testing easier down the line.

a project, which again is usually a pretty good thing.

--- The Expiration Service ---

Well, we are all done with our orders and ticket service for now.
We've got a bunch of publishers, listeners wrote handlers inside of both them.
At this point, there's definitely a couple of different directions we could go.
We could go back over to our client project and start to put together the front end for creating orders

and we're only going to revisit the React application when just about all of our back end stuff is done.
That is the real focus of this course overall.
It is really the back end component as opposed to just kind of juggling data in the world of React.
So on the back and side, what is the next thing we're going to do?
Well, we're going to take a look at that idea of expiring an order after some period of time.
So this is going to be referred to as the expiration service.
This service is going to have one single job.
It is going to watch for order created coming in.
So we're going to definitely implement a listener inside there.
And then after that 15 minute timer or however long we eventually configure it to be, we're going to
have the expiration service, then publish an event of its own called simply expiration complete.
The goal of this event right here is to tell the order service that one of its orders has now expired.
Now, one thing I want to really highlight, that's in this diagram right here, the expiration service
is not responsible for telling the rest of the world.
Then order has been canceled.
That's not his job.
Its sole purpose is to have that 15 minute timer.
It is then up to the order service to take a look at this event and decide whether or not it is actually
time to cancel an order.
This is really important because when this event comes in to the order service, a user may have already
paid for an order and we might have not gone over to the expiration service and told it that the order
was paid for and that it should cancel that timer.
So all this service really does for us listen to order created emit expiration complete after 15 minutes
or so the service is going to be pretty straightforward in nature and certainly a lot easier to put
together than all the other services we put together.
So far.
It's not going to have any root handlers, won't have any express server, nothing like that.
It's really just a listener and a publisher.
Now, having said all that, of course, there's always some hidden complexity.
Always, always, always.
So the real question about the service comes down to how are we going to let that 15 minute timer elapse?
How are we going to keep track of it, and how are we going to make sure that we emit an event precisely
15 minutes after?
Oh, that's a big question.
We've got a couple of different options available to us.
So let's take a pause right here.
We're going to take a look at four or five, I think four different options of how we can implement
that timer inside the expiration service.

--- Expiration Options ---

In this video, we're going to take a look at a couple of different ways of making sure the expiration
service waits about the 15 minutes or so before emitting that expiration complete event.
The first thing we want to do is really just kind of picture that service in isolation.
The idea here is order created comes in and then we're going to have some mechanism inside of here to
wait that 15 minutes or so and then eventually emit some event of expiration complete.
Now I keep talking about waiting 15 minutes and all that stuff, just as a very quick reminder if we
think back.
So when we actually create an order and where we assign that timer, if we go back to our order service,
take a look at routes and then new TS.
Inside of here.
You'll recall that our mechanism for actually tracking when order expires is a timestamp.
So that is the time at some point in time in the future when this order is going to expire.
So when I talk about waiting 15 minutes or something like that, it's really not so much waiting for
15 minutes, so much as it is waiting for this timestamp to go from being in the future into the past.
In other words, when it is this time indicated by this timestamp right here, that's when we want to
emit this expiration complete event.
Having said that, as we're discussing this service, I'm really just going to keep saying, oh, yeah,
we want to wait 15 minutes or so.
Let's not technically we are waiting 15 minutes inside the service.
It is really technically at some future point in time that is indicated inside of this event.
We want to emit that event of expiration complete.
So with that little disclaimer out of the way, what are the ways that we can actually implement this?
Well, the first one that we're going to take a look at, really simple, super basic, we could say
this is totally an option, but there is a big downside to it.
We could say that whenever we see this event come in, we could just use something like set time out
so we can have some set time out function.
We tell it to wait 15 minutes.
Now, that's not actually valid right there.
We cannot give a set time out a string of 15 minutes, but you get the idea.
We could provide some number of milliseconds to wait, and after that number of milliseconds, we can
have some code inside of here to publish the expiration complete event.
And this definitely is an option, but it's not super viable.
The reason that it's not a great option is that set time out stores a timer in memory.
So if our expiration service were to ever restart for any reason whatsoever, then all the timers that
we have running at that point in time are going to be lost and we're going to completely forget about
the fact that, well, we have to publish the expiration complete event in some remaining amount of
time.
So this would be super simple in nature, but a very clear downside to it.
So what's another option?
Well, the second option we have available to us.
Would be to just set up a listener for order created.

we can just not ask the incoming message.
If we do not act this incoming event, remember acknowledge it.
That means that Nats is going to automatically re deliver this thing 5 seconds in the future.
And so we could just rely upon that constant re delivery and every single time we could just check the
expires at time.
And whenever it's in the past we can say okay time to actually act this event finally and publish our

And this is also, without a doubt, a viable option.
We could definitely put something like this together, but there is a pretty big downside to this.

So in other words, we might have other events that we are having trouble processing inside of our app.

And then maybe after we have tried to process them say five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten times,
we might then throw some kind of critical alert to our engineers and say, Hey, there's some event

And so if we are relying upon this kind of a re delivery mechanism for both logging purposes and for

--- What's Bull All About? ---

In this video, we're going to get a better idea of the Bugs library and how it works with Reddit server
and then eventually understand how we're going to use it inside of our project.
Okay.
So in this diagram, this is not what we are doing with Bull.
This is a diagram of what people traditionally use bull for.
So I just want you to understand a little bit of background about this library.
So in this imaginary scenario right here, we might have an application where a user can make a request
with the intent to convert some video file from one format, such as an MP four to another format such
as MKV.
If you are not familiar with these file format for video, no problem whatsoever is just an example.
All I mean to say is that this request, in order to fulfill it, we need a lot of processing power.
Now, rather than doing a conversion task like this on some immediate web server, we will very frequently
instead have some kind of worker server, some separate machine, some separate container or something
else inside of our app that is completely standalone and separate from the web server.
The goal of this worker server is to have some actual video conversion process go on.
In this diagram, I'm showing just one worker server, but we might very easily have multiple copies
of this worker server like so.
Whenever someone makes this incoming request right here to our web server, it's going to queue something
called a job.
A job is really nothing more than a plain JavaScript object.
It describes some amount of processing that needs to be done on some particular thing.
Well, it's going to send this job object over to this Reddit server where Reddit is going to store
this list of jobs.
Then each of these different worker servers are going to consistently pull this right of server and
wait for some job to appear.
As soon as some job shows up, this worker is going to pull that job off, do some processing on it,
and then send a message back over to Reddit's to say that the processing is complete.
That's it.
That's what bull is really used for.
Now, just be really clear.
Bull gets used both on this web server over here and inside of each of these worker servers as well.
SAPOL is really handling the entire process, everything from setting up the initial job to processing
it to sending back some notification to say that the job is complete.
In this respect.
This entire read server and bull thing might actually seem kind of similar to our entire event processing
setup with Nat streaming server and the node NAT streaming client that we are using.
They are somewhat similar in nature.
However, we would not really want to use bul or doing the kind of event processing that you and I are
doing or the kind of async messaging between our different services.
The reason for that is that bull is simply not designed for it.
Well, it's designed for kind of one off little jobs.
It's not really intended to be handling a vast or huge number of messages as that streaming server is.
Okay.
So now just a little couple more pieces of terminology around bull.
So when we start to make use of bull, just one additional piece of terminology I want to add inside
of here, we're going to create something called a queue.
A queue is essentially the main abstraction inside a bull.
A Q represents some series of messages that we want to queue up.
And eventually process over time.
So we're going to use pull to specifically create a queue.
When we create the key, we're also going to specify exactly what we want to do with messages that are
flowing through it.
And finally, here's essentially what's going to be going on inside of our app.
So in our case, we do not have any separate worker server.
Everything is contained entirely inside the expiration service.
So for us, this web server right here and the worker server over here are really just one single server
and we're really just making use of bull for this kind of delayed messaging aspect and to make sure
that if the expiration service ever goes down, chances are the server will not also go down.
Hopefully it won't anyways.
So that's where you really using Bull and red is for inside this project.

--- Emitting the Order Cancelled Event ---

complete.

The ticket that is associated with it is going to be considered to be no longer reserved.

ticket it had been associated with.

buy.

wondering, what were these orders for?
I don't have any information.

--- Payments Flow with Stripe ---

We've now got everything around handling orders put together inside of our payment service.
So now our attention is going to move over to actually handling credit cards and actually billing users.
So in this video, we're going to get an overview of the API that we're going to use to eventually handle
real credit card payments coming in from our users.
All right.
So a quick diagram.
First off, we're going to start with a quick mockup of what a user is going to see in our app.
On the left hand side is a very simplified version of what a user is going to look at whenever they
take a look at an individual ticket.
So this would be a ticket that a user might want to buy.
So we're going to display the title of The Ticket and the Price.
And then right after that, we'll show a Buy Now button or something that looks very similar.
Whenever a user clicks on this, we're going to use a third party library to open up a automatic dialog
that looks like this right here.
This is going to be a dialog created by a third party library called the Stripe JS Library.
The goal of this modal dialog right here is to take in some credit card input from a user.
The user will enter in their name and then a credit card number and then submit the payment.
So this entire modal right here again is created by Stripe JS And the reason I'm saying that so much
is that what happens with this information is really important for us to understand.
At no point in time do you and I really want to directly handle credit card numbers, and that's what
this Stripe API does for us.
It removes the requirement of you and I to deal with credit card numbers directly because there are
huge security concerns with handling credit cards at any point in time.
So by having this modal window right here created by Stripe, we're essentially delegating, handling
everything related to a credit card number off to a stripe, as opposed to dealing with it ourselves.
So what happens when the user clicks on submit right there?
Well, let's take a look at another diagram and understand what happens when a user submits their credit
card number.
Okay.
So this diagram is a little bit complicated, even though it looks relatively simple in nature because
there's kind of a lot of hidden gotchas and hidden little steps inside of here.
So we're going to have running inside the browser the Stripe JS library.
That is the thing that is going to eventually create that modal window.
Users can enter in their credit card details and when they click on Submit, the Stripe JS Library is
going to take those credit card details and send them off to the Stripe API.
Now during this initial send off right here, we're essentially going to get back something called a
token.
And you should really view this token right here as kind of like an authorization.
It is something that is going to allow you and I, some developers to eventually charge that credit
card that the user just submitted for some amount of money.
The token that is received back inside the browser when those credit card details are submitted, should
be thought of as a pre authorization.
No money has been charged yet.
It is a token that allows us to do a follow up request and actually charge some real money.
The nice thing about this token is that it is a little bit more secure than handling a credit card number
directly.
It's really a kind of one time use thing where as soon as we charge some money with that token, that's
it.
We no longer have any access to the user's credit card or anything like that.
The token is going to be sent back into the browser from the Stripe API.
The Stripe JS library is again going to take that token and hand it off to you and I.
Inside of our JavaScript code that is also being executed inside the browser.
You and I are then going to take that token and submit it inside a request to our payments service.
Then inside of our payment service, you and I are going to take that token.
We're going to make sure that the user is trying to pay for some valid order.
We're going to make sure we verify the price correctly, all that kind of stuff.
And then once we decide that it's now time to charge the user's credit card.
We're going to make a request from our payment service off to the Stripe API, and we're going to include
that token.
And that's what's going to actually finalize the charge or really create a charge.
The term charge in the world of Stripe really means payment.
So whenever you see a charge, we're talking about a credit card charge or a payment of sorts.
So it's only when you and I take that token and make the final request to the Stripe API that the user's
credit card actually gets charged.
And you and I, in theory, receive some money.
Now, as we look at this diagram right here, you're going to notice that the browser component plays
well, a really big part of this entire flow.

--- Don't Cancel Completed Orders! ---

There is one other small change we're going to make to our exploration complete listener.
So right now, whenever we receive a message, we're going to find the corresponding order no matter
what, and always mark the order as being cancelled.
And as you can imagine, there might be a kind of big downside to this.
What would happen if we received a cancellation event around an order that has already been paid for?
Well, chances are we would take this order that has already been paid for or be marked as complete
and cancel it anyways.
So we do have to add in a little check here and just make sure that we do not try to cancel an order
that has been paid for right after our little check to make sure that we have an order.
We're going to take a look at the order status property and we're going to say that if this is equal
to order status dot complete, then let's just return early act the message because we do not want to
do anything with this cancellation event.
So I'm going to return early and call message back leg.
So.
Okay.
Good little fix.

--- Development Workflow ---

Our project is now looking pretty good and now it's time for us to actually deploy it.
This is going to be a lot of fun.
We're going to walk through the process of creating a production style deployment pipeline.
And when we talk about deployment, it's not really just about making sure that our code is live somewhere.
Instead, it's about the entire workflow and how we make sure that we can make changes somehow.
Save those changes and make sure those changes get deployed somewhere automatically.
So we're going to build out an entire workflow process here.
We're not just going to look alone at doing the deployment stuff.
All right.
So, of course, a couple of quick diagrams.
So here's the entire idea.
At some point in time, you might have multiple different teams working on a single product.
These two teams might be working on very different services.
And after they make some changes to the services, we should expect that those changes will be eventually
deployed into some production Kubernetes cluster.
So we need a workflow to make sure that multiple teams can be working on the same project at the same
time and eventually merge all these changes together and deploy them in some meaningful fashion without
having some nasty conflicts or errors along the way.
So I'm going to show you a little diagram or a workflow that I've personally used in many projects,
and I know many, many other engineers use in projects as well.
It's a pretty foolproof diagram or really workflow.
The first time you learn it, it's a little bit confusing, but once you understand the idea behind
it, the workflow is pretty bulletproof and it's going to work in the vast, vast majority of scenarios.
Okay, so here it is.
So this is the overall diagram.
I'm going to zoom in and we're going to walk through it step by step.
So we're starting off on your local machine where you are going to be working on some changes to some
particular service.
So we're going to imagine that you are making a change to, say, the ticket service after you have
made your changes.
You are then going to commit that code or those changes to a git branch.
So we're going to create a branch with Git.
We're going to commit all of our changes to that branch.
The only requirement here is that we make changes and we commit them to any branch besides the master
branch.
We're going to treat the master branch as a very special branch in this workflow.
After we have committed those changes will then push that branch up to GitHub.
Then our workflow jumps over to GitHub.
GitHub is going to receive that updated branch.
You are then going to manually create a pull request through the github UI.
A polar request is a request to essentially merge some changes from one branch into another branch.
In this case, we're going to make a polar request to merge changes from the branch you just created
into the master branch.
The instant that we create that pull request, we are going to configure GitHub to automatically run
all the tests inside of our project.
So by just creating this pull request, we're going to make sure that GitHub runs all those different
tests we have created over time.
After all those tests pass, we are then going to merge our pull request into the master branch.
Like I said, the master branch is going to be a very special branch inside of our app.
Whenever we make a change to the master branch, we're going to configure GitHub so that it automatically
deploys all of our changes to our live Kubernetes cluster.
And you'll notice that in this entire workflow, we haven't really said that much about deployment or
where we are deploying our app to.
So this is really a very generic general workflow that you can use to deploy code to any kind of target,
be it Google Cloud, AWS or anything else.

--- Git Repository Approaches ---

In this video, we're going to create a new git repository inside of our project.
Before we do, however, I want to have just a quick note, one or two on how we create Git and use
Git inside of a microservices project.
So in general, you're going to see that there are two different styles of managing code in a microservices
project using Git or really any other version control.
One approach is to use what is referred to as a mono repo.
This is where we are going to create a single git repository to track all the changes made to all of
our different services.
So in this scenario, all of our code lives inside of one single git repository.
The other approach is to create a separate repository for each individual service.
So we're going to have one git repository for auth, another for tickets payments.
So on you get the idea.
You're going to see that even though it might make a lot of sense when you initially think about this,
it might seem like it makes a lot of sense to create a single git repository for each repo but or for
each service.
But you're going to see that in reality what a lot of different companies do and I'm talking about very,
very large companies with tremendously large code bases, they actually trend towards using a single
repository to track all the code inside of their project.
One of the biggest reasons for this is that every single time that you create a new git repository,
there's actually a lot of overhead that goes along with that.
You have to create a separate repository on, say, GitHub or get lab depending on what service you're
using.
You might have to create a separate set of authentication keys just to get access to that repository,
you have to set up a separate CI and CD pipeline.
There's a lot of work that goes into creating each of these Git repositories when we're working with
microservices.
It's not really just as simple as writing out Git in it and saying, okay, that's it, we're done.
Instead, there really is a lot of work.
So to limit that amount of overhead.
Very simple solution.
Just use one single git repository.
And that's not to say that there are no downsides of using a single repository, because there definitely
are.
As a matter of fact, we're going to run into a couple of those downsides as we go through this deployment
workflow.
In this course because the vast majority of larger companies doing micro services use a single git repository.
We're going to take that same pattern.
So we're going to use a single git repository to track all of our different services.

--- Adding a CI Test Script ---

In the last video, we created our first GitHub hook.
We're now going to try to test this thing out.
So our ultimate goal is to be able to create a pull request and see all the tests for specifically our
service get executed.
Now, one thing I want to point out is that inside this little script we put in NPM, run test, colon
PSI.
So why is that?
Well, whenever we run our tests inside of this GitHub environment, we need to make sure that our test
suite exits automatically at some point in time.
Right now, our NPM run test command is going to start up just inside the watcher mode.
So it's going to run continuously just watching for changes to be made to our source code.
We do not want that when we're running our tests on GitHub.
We want just one run of our test suite and we want to exit entirely.
So rather than running NPM test directory directly, we're going to instead create a new script called
Test Colon PSI.
That is going to run our test suite exactly one time and then automatically exit.

--- The Deployment Plan ---

Our digital ocean cluster is up and running, we can connect to it and now it's time to start to deploy
our application to it.
I'm going to show you a diagram very quickly that's going to outline how we are going to use a GitHub
action workflow to automatically deploy all of our different services to this running cluster.
So the first time we look at this diagram, it's going to be a little bit confusing.
So let me walk you through it.
Each of these vertical series right here.
So we've got one vertical series right there, another one right there and so on, represents a different
workflow file that we're going to put together, or essentially a separate GitHub action.
So in total, we're going to have about seven different workflow files.
In each of these different workflow files, we are going to have a little bit of configuration that's
going to run any time that we merge a pull request into the master branch.
Whenever we merge a pull request into the master branch, we're going to inspect each of our different
services so the service client expiration and so on.
And if anything had changed inside of that service or specifically inside of our folder, client folder,
expiration folder and so on, then we're going to go through the series of steps that you see on the
right hand side.
So long story short, just to repeat that one more time, because this is a confusing diagram.
Every time that we merge a polar request into the master branch, we're going to see if anything changed
inside of that directory.
And if it did, we're going to go through this series of steps.
So that series of steps, we're going to first take everything inside that art directory and build a
new image out of it.
So that's a normal Docker image, similar to how we've done it many, many times in the past.
We're then going to take that image and push it off to Docker Hub.
After that, we're going to reach out to our running cluster.
So our cluster on digital ocean and we're going to update our deployment for the service and we're going
to tell that deployment to use the newest version of the auth image that is available, the one that
we had just pushed off to Docker Hub.
So that is it for each of our individual six services.
The actual workflow files or the GitHub action files are going to be almost identical in nature.
The reason we are creating all these workflow files separately is just so we can make sure that we do
not rebuild and deploy images if nothing has changed inside of a given service.
In addition, this is also going to make it really easy for us to change the building process for a
particular service if we need to at some point in time.
For example, we might decide to rewrite the payment service using a different programming language
at some point.
And so we would want to make sure that we could very easily customize how that payment service gets
built at some point.
And maybe we need to push it off to a different provider.
Who knows?
We can do that very easily by creating a separate workflow for each of our different services.
Now beyond each of our individual services.
Remember, we also have that set of Kubernetes config files, which is where we create all of our different
actual services, where we define our ingress service and where we also define all the different deployments
themselves.
So as an additional workflow, in addition to all these other six that we're going to put together,
we're going to have one other workflow that is always going to be executed at all times.
And we're going to make sure that we reach into that infra directory.
And we're going to apply all the YAML files inside there to our cluster.
Remember that?
The infra directory.
Right here is where all of our Kubernetes config files live.
So if we make any changes to these config files, we're just going to reapply them to our cluster.

That's the general plan.
So total, we're got to create, well, seven different config files.

--- What is Docker? ---

In the last section, we tried to answer the question of why use Docker?

Any time you see someone refer to Docker in a blog post or an article or a forum or wherever it might
be, they're kind of making reference to an entire ecosystem of different projects, tools and pieces
of software.
So if someone says, Oh yeah, I use Docker on my project, they might be referring to Docker client
or Docker server.
They might be referring to Docker Hub or Docker Compose.
Again, these are all projects, tools, pieces of software that come together to form a platform or
ecosystem around creating and running something called containers.
And so your immediate question might be OC, well, what's a container?

entire course.

closely over time.
But right now, let me give you two important pieces of terminology.
When I ran that command, something called the Docker CLI reached out to something called the Docker
Hub, and it downloaded a single file called An Image.
An image is a single file containing all the dependencies and all the configuration required to run
a very specific program.
For example, Redis, which is what the image that I just downloaded was supposed to run.
This is a single file that gets stored on your hard drive, and at some point in time you can use this
image to create something called a container.
A container is an instance of an image, and you can kind of think of it as being like a running program.
We're going to go into great detail over time, over behind her to learn exactly how a container works.
Exactly.
But right now, all we really need to understand is that a container is a program with its own isolated
set of hardware resources.
So it kind of has its own little set or its own little space of memory as its own little space of networking
technology and its own little space of hard drive space as well.
So I didn't really answer the question here of what Docker is, but we did learn at least that a reference
to Docker is really talking about a whole collection of different projects and tools.

--- But Really... What's a Container? ---

In the last section.
We continue to talk a little bit about images, but we're still surprisingly light on some of the details
around exactly what a container is.
So in this section, I'm going to give you a behind the scenes look at what a container is and how it
is created on your machine.
Now, to understand a container, you first need to have a little bit of background on exactly how your
operating system runs on your computer.
So I'm going to first give you a quick overview of your operating system.
Okay.
So this is a quick overview of the operating system on your computer.
Most operating systems have something called a kernel.
This kernel is a running software process that governs access between all the programs that are running
on your computer and all the physical hardware that is connected to your computer as well.
So if you're at the top of this diagram, we have different programs that your computer is running,
such as Chrome or Terminal Spotify or Node.js.
If you've ever made use of Node.js before and you've written a file to the hard drive, it's technically
not Node.js that is speaking directly to the physical device.
Instead, Node.js says to your kernel, Hey, I want to write a file to the hard drive.
The kernel then takes that information and eventually persists it to the hard disk.
So the kernel is always kind of this intermediate layer that governs access between these programs and
your actual hard drive.
The other important thing to understand here is that these running programs interact with the kernel
through things called system calls.
These are essentially like function invocations.
The kernel exposes different endpoints to say, Hey, if you want to write a file to the hard drive,
call this endpoint or this function right here.
It takes some amount of information and then that information will be eventually written to the hard
disk or memory or whatever else is required.
Now thinking about this entire system right here, I want to pose a kind of hypothetical situation to
you.
I want you to imagine for just a second that you and I have two programs running on our computer.
Maybe one of them is Chrome, like Chrome, the web browser, and the other is Node.js, the JavaScript
server side runtime.
I want you to imagine that we're in a crazy world where Chrome, in order to work properly, has to
have Python version two installed and Node.js has to have version three installed.
However, on our hard disk, we only have access to Python version two.
And for whatever crazy reason, we are not allowed to have two identical installations of Python at
the same time.
So as it stands right now, Chrome would work properly because it has access to version two, but Node.js
would not because we do not have a version or a copy of Python version three.
Again, this is a completely make believe situation.
I just want you to kind of consider this for a second, because this is kind of leading into what a
container is.
So how could we solve this issue?
Well, one way to do it would be used to make use of a operating system feature known as name spacing.
With name spacing, we can look at all of the different hardware resources connected to our computer,
and we can essentially segment out portions of those resources.
So we could create a segment of our hard disk specifically dedicated to housing Python version two.
And we could make a second segment specifically dedicated to housing Python version three.
Then to make sure that Chrome has access to this segment over here and Node.js has access to this segment
over here, any time that either them issues a system call to read information off the hard drive the
kernel will look at that incoming system call and try to figure out which process it is coming from.
So the kernel could say, okay, if Chrome is trying to read some information off the harddrive, I'm
going to direct that call over to this little segment of the hard disk over here, the segment that
has Python version two and Node.js.
Any time that makes a system call to read the hard drive, the kernel can redirect that over to this
segment for Python version three.
And so by making use of this kind of name spacing or segmenting feature, we can have the ability to
make sure that Chrome and Node.js are able to work on the same machine.
Now, again, in reality, neither of these actually needed installation of Python.
This is just a quick example.
So this entire process of kind of segmenting a hard or a hardware resource based on the process that
is asking for it is known as name spacing.
With name spacing, we are allowed to isolate resources per a process or a group of processes.
And we're essentially saying that any time a this particular process asks for a resource, we're going
to direct it to this one little specific area of the given piece of hardware.
Now, name spacing is not only used for hardware, it can be also used for software elements as well.
So for example, we can namespace a process to restrict the area of a hard drive that is available or
the network devices that are available, or the ability to talk to other processes or the ability to
see other processes.
These are all things that we can use name spacing for to essentially limit the resources or kind of
redirect requests for resources from a particular process.
Very closely related to this idea of name spacing is another feature called control groups.
A control group can be used to limit the amount of resources that a particular process can use.
So name spacing is for saying, Hey, this area of the hard drive is for this process.
A control group can be used to limit the amount of memory that a process can use, the amount of CPU,
the amount of hard drive, input input or input output, and the amount of network bandwidth as well.
So these two features put together can be used to really kind of isolate a single process and limit
the amount of resources it can talk to and the amount of bandwidth essentially that it can make use
of.
As you might imagine, this entire kind of little section right here, this entire vertical of a running
process, plus this little segment of a resource that it can talk to is what we refer to as a container.
And so when people say, Oh yeah, I have a Docker container, you really should not think of these
as being like a physical construct that exists inside of your computer.
Instead, a container is really a process or a set of processes that have a grouping of resources specifically
assigned to it.
And so this is a diagram that we're going to be looking at quite a bit.
Any time that we think about a container, we've got some running process that sends a system call to
a kernel.
The kernel is going to look at that incoming system call and direct it to a very specific portion of
the hard drive, the RAM, CPU or whatever else it might need.
And a portion of each of these resources is made available to that singular process.
Now, the last question you might have here is, och, well, I get what a container is, but with that
in mind, what is the real relation between one of those containers or that kind of singular, singular
process and grouping of resources to an image?
How is that single file eventually create this container?
That's a good question.
One more quick diagram.
Any time that we talk about an image, we're really talking about a file system snapshot.
So this is essentially kind of like a copy paste of a very specific set of directories or files.
And so we might have an image that contains just Chrome and Python.
An image will also contain a specific startup command.
So here's what happens behind the scenes when we take an image and turn it into a container.
First off, the kernel is going to isolate a little section of the harddrive and make it available to
just this container.
And so we can kind of imagine that after that little subset is created, the file snapshot inside the
image is taken and placed into that little segment of the hard drive.
And so now inside of this very specific grouping of resources, we've got a little section of the hard
drive that has just chrome and python installed and essentially nothing else.
The start up command is then executed, which we can kind of imagine in this case is like start up chrome,
just run chrome for me.
And so chrome is invoked.
We create a new instance of that process and that created process is then isolated to this set of resources
inside the container.
So that's pretty much it.
That is the relationship between a container and an image, and it's how an image is eventually taken
and turn into a running container.
Now there's still a tremendous amount more to learn about containers and images.
So let's take a quick break and continue in the next section.

So name spacing control groups belong to Linux, not to Windows, not to Mac OS.

running processes inside of containers.
And it's that Linux kernel that's going to be in charge of limiting access or kind of constraining access

--- Stopping Containers ---

In all these commands we've been running with Docker, Create and Start.
There's kind of one oddity that I want to show you really quickly.
Let's do a container creation and then a start and you'll see some kind of weird behavior.
I'm going to run Docker, create busy box, and then we're going to set up that ping command again.
So I'll say ping google.com that's going to create the container.
I can then copy the ID right here and do Docker start and paste that ID and you'll notice that I did
not put in the dash a so I have not attached this container.
When I run that command I see the ID of the container echoed back to me and then I can do a docker logs
and paste that ID in and I'll see that.
Yep.
It is in fact running the ping command and if I do the Docker command, I can see that container is
running and it's continuing to execute the ping command.
Now there's just one kind of odd thing here.
How do we actually stop this container?
Remember, the ping command is going to essentially go on forever and we have to actually send it a
signal until it.
Hey, Ping command, please stop like you're all done.
No need to reach out to Google anymore.
So we need to figure out a way to stop this running container.
In the past, we've just been hitting control C on our keyboard, or we've allowed the container to
automatically stop itself, as was the case with the Echo Command.
So in order to stop a container that seems to be running amok on its own, we can issue either the Docker
Stop Command or the Docker Kill Command.
Both.
These are going to stop the running container, but they look like they kind of do the same thing here.
So what's the difference between them?
Well, here's what happens behind the scenes.
When you issue a Docker stop command, a hardware signal is sent to the process or the primary process
inside that container.
In the case of Docker, stop, we send a sig term message which is short for terminate signal.
It's a message that's going to be received by the process, telling it essentially to shut down on its
own time.
Sig term is used any time that you want to stop a process inside of your container and shut the container
down and you want to give that process inside there a little bit of time to shut itself down and do
a little bit of cleanup.
A lot of different programming languages have the ability for you to listen for these signals inside
of your code base.
And as soon as you get that signal, you could attempt to do a little bit of cleanup or maybe save some
file or emit some message or something like that.
On the other hand, the Docker kill command issues a sig kill or kill signal to the primary running
process inside the container.
Sick kill essentially means you have to shut down right now and you do not get to do any additional
work.
So ideally we always stop a container with the Docker stop command in order to get the running process
inside of it a little bit of time to shut itself down.
Otherwise, if it feels like the container has locked up and it's not responding to the Docker stop
command, then we could issue Docker kill instead.
Now, one kind of little oddity or interesting thing about Docker stop.
When you issue Docker, stop to a container.
If the container does not automatically stop in 10 seconds, then Docker is going to automatically fall
back to issuing the Docker Kill Command.
So essentially Docker stop is us being nice, but it has only got 10 seconds to actually shut down.
So let's now try using these commands on that kind of runaway container that we have right now.
So again, do Docker PS and I'll see that the ping Google Command or simply ping google.com container
is still running.
So I'm going to take the ID right there and I'll issue a Docker stop and then I'll paste that ID in.
And then we're going to wait and notice how we're kind of waiting here.
We're going to end up waiting just about 10 seconds.
We're waiting 10 seconds because it turns out that the ping command does not properly respond to a sig
term message.
The ping command doesn't really have the ability to say, Oh, yeah, I understand you want me to shut
down the ping command is rather I don't know what's the term for it.
The ping command wants to do its own thing and it just wants to run forever.
And so after we waited those 10 seconds, eventually the kill signal was sent to it, telling it, Hey,
Ping, you're done.
Get out of here.
Shut yourself down.
And so that's why we had to wait a couple of seconds.
Let's now take that container ID again.
We're going to start the container back up and try killing it this time with using Docker kill.
So I'll first start the container back up with Docker Start and I'll paste the ID in and then I'll issue
a Docker kill and paste the ID again and this time you're going to see that's it.
Instantly dead.
No grace, period.
Just get out of here.
All right, so that's it.
That's the two commands that we're going to use for closing down containers that are running.
Remember, you can always get the idea of the container ahead of time with Docker.
PS, you can copy the ID and then run either Docker Stop or Docker kill.
And in general, I do recommend use Docker stop to give the processes inside there a chance to shut
down.
And if they don't shut down nicely, nicely, as we saw with the ping command, eventually Docker is
going to fall back to issuing a kill on the container instead.
All right.

--- The Purpose of the 'it' Flag ---

In the last section, we found that we were able to connect to Rita Sealy inside of our running Docker
container and notice how mine is still running over here on the second window by adding on the dash
it flag.
So when I did that, we saw, yep, we got this prompt here, we could enter stuff in.
I could then press control, see to exit back out.
However, if I tried running this command without the TX flag.
It appeared that I just got kicked directly back over to my terminal.
So in this section, I want to give you a better idea of what this dash flag right here is really doing
for us.
The first thing you need to understand is a little bit more about how processes run inside of a Linux
environment.
As a quick reminder, when you are running Docker on your machine, every single container that you
are running is running inside of a virtual machine running Linux.
So these processes are really being executed inside of a Linux world, even if you're on Mac or Windows.
All right.
So with that in mind.
In this diagram, we've got three different running processes all inside in theory of a running container
or a really inside of a Linux environment.
Every process that we create in a Linux environment has three communication channels attached to it
that we refer to as standard in, standard out and standard air.
These channels are used to communicate information either into the process or out of the process.
Standard in, as you might guess, is used to communicate information into the process.
So when you are at your terminal and you type stuff in the stuff you type is being directed in to a
running standard and channel attached to say theoretically the standard out channel that is attached
to any given process is going to convey information that is coming from the process.
So standard out might be redirected over to your running terminal and that's going to end up as being
stuff that is going to show up on the screen.
Standard error is very similar, but it conveys information out of the process that is kind of like
an error in nature.
So if radically has some error inside of it, that's going to be communicated to the outside world over
the standard error channel and very similar to standard out, that's going to be redirected to show
up on the screen of your terminal.
So how does that relate to the flag when we do the Docker exec dash it?
Well, the it right here is actually two separate little flags.
In reality, it's a dash I and a dash T like so.
But by convention, we usually just kind of shorten it down to be simply it, which is 100% equivalent
to the two separate flags.
The dash I on here means when we execute this new command inside the container, we want to attach our
terminal to the standard end channel of that new running process.
So by adding on the dash flag, we are saying make sure that any stuff that I type gets directed to
standard in of Rita cli.
The flag is what kind of makes all this checks to show up a little bit pretty.
Now, in reality, it's doing a little bit more than that.
But at the end of the day, the real effect that the dash ti flag is to make sure that all the text
that you are entering in and that is coming out shows up in a nicely formatted manner on your screen.
And again, it's doing a little bit more behind the scenes than that.
But at the end of the day, that's kind of its effect.
Let's try attaching or doing our Docker exec on the running container one more time and leaving off
the dash t flag and just seeing what happens.
So I'll do a Docker PS to get my containers ID again.
Then I'll do a Docker exec and then we'll do only dash I.

I can still run that command though, and I still see OC and I can still do get my value and I still

But again, all, all this stuff is not nicely formatted.
And so that's kind of the purpose more or less kind of simplifying things here.
Just a little bit of that Dashti flag.
So that's pretty much it.
That's the purpose of it.

--- Creating Docker Images ---

Throughout this course, we've been making use of images that have been created by other engineers.
So, for example, we have used, say, the Hello World Image or Redis or Busy Box.
These are all images that were created by other engineers.
We download them onto our local machine and then created a container out of them.
At this point, we're going to start to figure out how we can build our own custom images so that we
can run our own applications inside of our own personalised containers.
The process for making an image is somewhat straightforward.
Like all things, you just have to learn a little bit of syntax.
So here's what we're going to do to make our own image.
We're going to create something called a Docker file.
A darker file is essentially a plain text file that is going to have a couple of lines of configuration
placed inside of it.
This configuration is going to define how our container behaves, or more specifically, what different
programs it's going to contain and what it does when it starts up as a container.
Once we create that Docker file, we'll then pass it off to the Docker client, which you will recall
is the Docker CLI that we've been using at our terminal.
In turn, the Docker client will provide the file to the Docker server.
The Docker server is what is doing the heavy lifting for us.
It's going to take the Docker file, look at all the lines of configuration that we have inside of it,
and then build a usable image that can then be used to start up a new container.
Now that Docker file is where all the complexity is going to sit.
And like I just said a moment ago, it's not really going to be the worst thing in the world.
It's just about learning a couple of new commands, that's all.
In fact, just about every Docker file that you and I are going to put together is almost always going
to look the same.
Inside of every Docker file, we're always going to specify a base image and we'll talk about what that
means in just a moment.
It's got it's going to be one of the first things we have to do.
After that, we'll add in some additional configuration to run commands, to add in some dependencies
or some more software, some more programs that we need to successfully create and execute our container.
And then finally, we will specify a startup command for the image.
So any time we take that image and create a container out of it, it will be the command that is executed
to essentially boot up or start the container.
It's the same command that we've been talking about around all of these images all along.
So that's it.
That's all we have to do to make our own image essentially just revolves around writing a Docker file.
So let's take a quick pause right here.
We'll come back the next section and get started working on our Docker file.

We don't see any fetch, we don't see any installation of dependencies.

In other words, it knows without a doubt that it's going to get the same image from the previous step

Redis.
It's already generated an image out of that step.
This image right here and this image has been cached and stored on your local machine.
So rather than going through the process of creating another container out of the alpine image and running
apk add update redis inside that container a second time, it says, You know what, I've already done
this work.
I'm just going to use the image that I generated during the previous step again.
But then after that, Docker correctly sees that there is a new command in play.
And this is not an update, right?
It's an update, TCC.
It sees that there's a new command right here, a new instruction in play.
And so from this point on, it decides, well, you know what, something has changed during the build
process.
We probably can't use our cache anymore.
And from here on out, we have to go through that process of generating a container and running a command
inside the container and taking the snapshot and going through all that stuff again.
Now, the interesting thing about this is that it has now executed run APK Ad GCSE and it has generated
an image out of that instruction right there.
So if we now run Docker, build a third time without making any changes to our Docker file, Docker
is going to correctly see we have made no changes to the Docker file.
None of these steps have changed whatsoever.
And so it's going to use the cached or saved versions of each of these images in building this new one.
Let's do that right now and you're going to see it in action.
So we're going to do Docker, build it a third time.
And you'll notice that bill process went extremely quickly.
So Docker correctly realised that it's already downloaded Alpine.
It's realized that it already ran the run command on top of Alpine.

cache version of that and it knows that it's already executed.
Command Right.
A server on top of the output of the GC step.
And so it's using the cache there again.
So the lesson to learn here is that any time that we make a change to our Docker file, we're going
to have to only rerun the series of steps from the change line on down.

So even though we're still taking the Alpine image and adding GC to it and adding Redis to it, the
series of steps have changed.
And so Docker is going to say, okay, well this time we're taking Alpine and first adding in GC scene.
So it will use the cache version of Alpine, but it's not going to have a cached version of the GC ad
to use because the last time that it ran that it added GC only after installing Redis.
So essentially the order of operations is different, so the cache cannot be used.
So I'm going to save this file after moving GC around and we'll try rebuilding our image for a fourth
time.
So I'll do Docker build dot, I'll run that and now you're going to see.
Yep, it has to go through that installation process all over again because the order of operations
have changed.
However, it only needs to rerun the steps from the change line on down, and so we have to rerun the
entire ad cc we rerun the entire ad redirects and we have to rerun the command server.
All right.
So again, if you are not changing your Docker file, that's great because it means that we can use
cache versions for building the image.
But the real lesson to learn here is that if you ever expect to have to change your Docker file, you
always want to put those changes like as far down as possible.
Now for right now, that might sound really confusing, but we're going to very quickly go through another
example in a couple of videos where you'll see that by changing the order of operations inside of our
Docker file can dramatically change how long it takes to rebuild our image.

--- Base Image Issues ---

By default, alpine is a very small image.
It's only about five megabytes large, and so it has a rather limited set of default programs included
inside of it.
In fact, I kind of like this diagram right here.
What programs are included in the alpine image?
Well, this is supposed to be a tumbleweed of sorts.
Not much.

You get a couple of very default Linux or Unix programs.
